revisions.message:
HTTP-RPC driver: tooz service discovery and fanout broadcaster

Adds service discovery and fanout relay to the HTTP-RPC driver.

Service discovery uses the tooz coordination library, giving operators a
single ``coordination_url`` option that supports memcached, etcd3, redis,
consul, Kubernetes, and file backends. The ToozServiceBroker registers
each listener as a group member with its endpoint and server-hostname
capabilities, and resolves RPC targets (including directed RPC) by
querying live group members. It is process-global with fork detection so
cotyledon-style workers each rebuild their own coordinator, uses a
background heartbeat thread, caches lookups for cache_max_age seconds,
and performs a single batched get_members_with_capabilities fetch to
avoid N+1 queries.

Fanout is handled by a standalone oslo-messaging-broadcaster service that
registers under the "fanout" name. The FanoutHandler relays each fanout
cast to all subscribers of the target topic using a thread-local httpx
client (avoiding cross-hub greenlet errors) and batched parallel
delivery. The broadcaster forces the threading oslo.service backend.

HTTPDriver now instantiates ToozServiceBroker directly. Adds the
oslo-messaging-broadcaster console script and tooz to the [http] extra.

Partially-implements: blueprint oslo-http-driver (2/3)

HTTP-RPC driver: tooz service discovery and fanout broadcaster

Adds service discovery and fanout relay to the HTTP-RPC driver.

Service discovery uses the tooz coordination library, giving operators a
single ``coordination_url`` option that supports memcached, etcd3, redis,
consul, Kubernetes, and file backends. The ToozServiceBroker registers
each listener as a group member with its endpoint and server-hostname
capabilities, and resolves RPC targets (including directed RPC) by
querying live group members. It is process-global with fork detection so
cotyledon-style workers each rebuild their own coordinator, uses a
background heartbeat thread, caches lookups for cache_max_age seconds,
and performs a single batched get_members_with_capabilities fetch to
avoid N+1 queries.

Fanout is handled by a standalone oslo-messaging-broadcaster service that
registers under the "fanout" name. The FanoutHandler relays each fanout
cast to all subscribers of the target topic using a thread-local httpx
client (avoiding cross-hub greenlet errors) and batched parallel
delivery. The broadcaster forces the threading oslo.service backend.

HTTPDriver now instantiates ToozServiceBroker directly. Adds the
oslo-messaging-broadcaster console script and tooz to the [http] extra.

failures are not replayed. The broadcaster forces the threading

HTTP-RPC driver: tooz service discovery and fanout broadcaster

Add broker-local tooz service discovery and the standalone fanout relay
to the HTTP-RPC driver. Each broker owns its coordinators, detects forks,
and uses one primary heartbeat thread in the normal case. An additional
listener in the same group gets a distinct coordinator and member ID.

Keep support for memcached, etcd3, Redis, and file backends through
coordination_url. When that option is unset, use the established
[oslo_messaging_http_consul] options and Consul catalog schema. Translate
those configuration names to the historical Tooz Consul URL names at the
broker boundary.

Consul discovery prefers the local datacenter and falls back to remote
datacenters. Fanout combines passing services from every datacenter.
Directed RPC uses a server-side Consul tag filter, which avoids transferring
a complete large service group. New registrations advertise HTTP/2, while
the client uses HTTP/1.1 for compatible preexisting entries during rolling
upgrades.

Use native Consul endpoint checks when possible. Other backends use the
client prober. Mutual-TLS deployments can opt in to native Consul checks
after the agent is configured with a trusted client certificate. Let Tooz
derive a safe Consul request timeout from membership_timeout unless the
operator sets an override.

Fanout is handled by oslo-messaging-broadcaster. It relays to all
subscribers with bounded parallel work and preserves stable message IDs for
safe pre-handoff retries. The broadcaster uses the threading oslo.service
backend.

Use the globally listed py-consul dependency for the default Consul
backend.

HTTP-RPC driver: tooz service discovery and fanout broadcaster

Add broker-local tooz service discovery and the standalone fanout relay to
the HTTP-RPC driver. Each broker owns its coordinators, detects forks, and
restores registrations after coordinator loss. Additional listeners in one
group use distinct coordinators and member IDs.

Support the standard tooz configuration names for memcached, etcd3, Redis,
file, and Consul coordination backends. When coordination_url is unset, use
the HTTP-RPC Consul options and the current Consul catalog schema. This driver
targets new deployments and does not add compatibility behavior for earlier
catalog schemas.

Consul discovery prefers the local datacenter and falls back to remote
datacenters. Fanout combines passing services from every datacenter. Directed
RPC uses a server-side Consul tag filter, which avoids transferring a complete
large service group. Discovery caches are bounded and report only data that
is within the configured stale interval.

Use native Consul endpoint checks when possible. Other backends use a
proxy-aware HTTP/1.1 health prober; RPC traffic continues to use HTTP/2.
Mutual-TLS deployments can opt in to native Consul checks after the agent has
a trusted client certificate. Let tooz derive a safe Consul request timeout
from membership_timeout unless the operator sets an override.

Fanout is handled by oslo-messaging-broadcaster. It discovers subscribers
before acceptance, applies bounded admission and parallel work, and preserves
stable message IDs for safe pre-handoff retries. Per-endpoint connection
timeouts bound stalled deliveries. The broadcaster uses the threading
oslo.service backend.

Use the globally listed py-consul dependency for the default Consul backend.

Adds the DevStack plugin, Zuul CI jobs, and operator/contributor
documentation for the HTTP-RPC driver.

The DevStack plugin disables RabbitMQ, installs the oslo.messaging[http]
extra with the appropriate tooz backend extra, generates an mTLS CA and
server/client certificates, overrides iniset_rpc_backend to write the
HTTP transport configuration for every service, and starts the
oslo-messaging-broadcaster. It selects the tooz coordination backend from
OSLO_RPC_TOOZ_URL and supports memcached, etcd3, redis, file, Kubernetes
(with namespace/RBAC/kubeconfig setup), and Consul (with a dev-mode
agent). Notifications are routed to Kafka.

Six experimental Zuul jobs run the full tempest suite against the driver,
one per tooz backend (memcached, etcd3, redis, file, k8s, consul), each
using Kafka for notifications and no RabbitMQ.

internals guide, wired into the admin and contributor toctrees, plus a
release note.

disable the client prober.

capacity guidance for Redis and the other supported Tooz backends. Correct
the broadcaster configuration group name.

and Consul, plus directed RPC and native-threading coverage.

kernel: add OPAE SDK userspace package for Debian trixie

Add a new userspace package, userspace/opae-sdk, that builds the Intel
OPAE SDK 2.14.0-3 for the Debian trixie layer. This is the userspace
companion to the in-tree Intel FPGA (DFL/OPAE) kernel enablement: it
provides the OPAE runtime, the development files and the extra FPGA
tools used to manage Intel FPGA / OPAE cards (e.g. Intel PAC N3000).

The source is the upstream release tarball
(https://github.com/OFS/opae-sdk/archive/refs/tags/2.14.0-3.zip). As it
is a .zip whose top-level directory is opae-sdk-2.14.0-3, a dl_hook
unzips it and renames the tree to <debname>-<debver> (opae-2.14.0-3),
mirroring the existing kernel-modules/intel-opae-fpga zip handling.

The Debian packaging under debian/trixie/deb_folder is derived from the
upstream packaging/opae/deb tree and adapted for the trixie toolchain:

- control: Maintainer switched to StarlingX, debhelper-compat (= 13),
  and the Build-Depends completed for an out-of-the-box build:
  pkg-config, pybind11-dev, libcli11-dev, libspdlog-dev and libnuma-dev
  (OPAE would otherwise FetchContent these, which debhelper disables),
  python3-jsonschema and python3-yaml (needed by the build-time
  ofs_parse.py generator), plus python3-pip/setuptools/wheel for the
  OPAE_BUILD_PYTHON_DIST stage.
- rules: set DEB_BUILD_OPTIONS=noddebs; reference the out-of-tree cmake
  build dir as obj-$(DEB_HOST_GNU_TYPE) instead of a hardcoded arch;
  pip-install the python dist artifacts with --break-system-packages and
  DEB_PYTHON_INSTALL_LAYOUT=deb_system so they land under /usr and
  dist-packages (PEP 668 / trixie). OPAE's cmake also stages those
  python packages under /usr/local, so the duplicate /usr/local tree is
  removed before packaging.
- opae-devel.install: add the cmake package-config exports
  (usr/lib/opae-2.14.0/*.cmake and modules/*.cmake) and the top-level
  usr/include/opae/cxx/core.h header, and resolve the @VERSION@
  placeholder in opae-devel.dirs to 2.14.0.

The package is registered for the trixie std build in
debian_trixie_pkg_dirs_std, and the three resulting binary packages
(opae, opae-devel, opae-extra-tools) are added to
debian_trixie_iso_image_std.inc.

Test Plan:
Pass: downloader - dl_hook unzips and renames to opae-2.14.0-3

OPAE SDK 2.14.0-3 for the Debian trixie layer. This is the userspace
companion to the in-tree Intel FPGA (DFL/OPAE) kernel enablement: it
provides the OPAE runtime, the development files and the extra FPGA
tools used to manage Intel FPGA / OPAE cards (e.g. Intel PAC N3000).

The source is the upstream release tarball
(https://github.com/OFS/opae-sdk/archive/refs/tags/2.14.0-3.zip). As it
is a .zip whose top-level directory is opae-sdk-2.14.0-3, a dl_hook
unzips it and renames the tree to <debname>-<debver> (opae-2.14.0-3),
mirroring the existing kernel-modules/intel-opae-fpga zip handling.

The Debian packaging under debian/trixie/deb_folder is derived from the
upstream packaging/opae/deb tree and adapted for the trixie toolchain:

- control: Maintainer switched to StarlingX, debhelper-compat (= 13),
  and the Build-Depends completed for an out-of-the-box build:
  pkg-config, pybind11-dev, libcli11-dev, libspdlog-dev and libnuma-dev
  (OPAE would otherwise FetchContent these, which debhelper disables),
  python3-jsonschema and python3-yaml (needed by the build-time
  ofs_parse.py generator), plus python3-pip/setuptools/wheel for the
  OPAE_BUILD_PYTHON_DIST stage.
- rules: set DEB_BUILD_OPTIONS=noddebs; reference the out-of-tree cmake
  build dir as obj-$(DEB_HOST_GNU_TYPE) instead of a hardcoded arch;
  pip-install the python dist artifacts with --break-system-packages and
  DEB_PYTHON_INSTALL_LAYOUT=deb_system so they land under /usr and
  dist-packages (PEP 668 / trixie). OPAE's cmake also stages those
  python packages under /usr/local, so the duplicate /usr/local tree is
  removed before packaging.
- opae-devel.install: add the cmake package-config exports
  (usr/lib/opae-2.14.0/*.cmake and modules/*.cmake) and the top-level
  usr/include/opae/cxx/core.h header, and resolve the @VERSION@
  placeholder in opae-devel.dirs to 2.14.0.

debian_trixie_pkg_dirs_std, and the three resulting binary packages
(opae, opae-devel, opae-extra-tools) are added to
debian_trixie_iso_image_std.inc.

revisions.message:
Add NVMe/FC transport to the NVMe-oF connector

Add Fibre Channel as a transport for the existing NVMe-oF connector,
selected by connection info with transport_type='fc'. FC portals carry
an "nn-0x<wwnn>:pn-0x<wwpn>" traddr (port unused); attach uses
"nvme connect --transport fc --traddr <target> --host-traddr <hba>",
iterating the local NVMe-capable FC HBAs. Native NVMe multipath (ANA)
assembles the paths, as for RoCE/TCP.

get_connector_properties now also reports host wwpns/wwnns when FC HBAs
are present (reusing the FC connector's WWN discovery) so NVMe/FC targets
can build the fabric zoning map. RoCE/TCP-only hosts are unchanged.

Change-Id: I0215aa3597b702d4ab2f4699c138e6dbb8ca6464
Signed-off-by: Simon Dodsley <simon@purestorage.com>

connect from (for example the nvme_fcloop loopback used in CI), the

active connection could be made and the target is FC, refresh the
controller names and re-check for a live controller before giving up,
and allow a couple more retries for the autoconnect to complete.

are present (reusing the FC connector's WWN discovery) so NVMe/FC targets
can build the fabric zoning map. RoCE/TCP-only hosts are unchanged.

revisions.message:
Allow non-CUSTOM traits in device profile groups

Cyborg's PCI and NVIDIA GPU drivers set the OWNER_CYBORG trait on
Placement resource providers, but the device profile API rejected
any trait not prefixed with CUSTOM_.  This meant users could not
round-trip the traits that Cyborg itself publishes into a device
profile request without first filtering them out.

The CUSTOM_ prefix check in _validate_post_request was overly
restrictive.  Removing it lets Placement remain the sole authority
on valid trait names, which is backward-compatible because
previously rejected requests now succeed and no existing valid
requests are affected.  No API microversion is needed since the
change only loosens validation.

The unit test is updated to verify that a device profile containing
trait:OWNER_CYBORG is accepted with a 200 response.  The DevStack
plugin now configures [cyborg] devices in tempest.conf for the
placement integration test introduced in the companion
cyborg-tempest-plugin change.

Closes-Bug: #2157586

Validate device profile traits against os-traits library

Cyborg's PCI and NVIDIA GPU drivers set standard traits such as
OWNER_CYBORG on Placement resource providers, but the device profile
API rejected any trait not prefixed with CUSTOM_.  Users could not
include these driver-published traits in a device profile request.

standard traits recognised by the os-traits library are now accepted
alongside CUSTOM_* traits, while genuinely unknown names are still
rejected with a clear error.  This is backward-compatible — previously
rejected requests now succeed and no existing valid requests are
affected — so no API microversion is needed.

the placement integration test introduced in the companion
cyborg-tempest-plugin change.

revisions.message:
Install the kerbside-proxy wheel into kerbside images.

Kerbside recently split out the proxying element which shovels SPICE
packets around from the python business logic and re-implemented
the high bandwidth proxy component in rust. The proxy is still pip
installable because of a maturin wrapper, and the kerbside package
depends on the kerbside-proxy package correctly.

However, it might be desirable for developers or deployers to be
able to optionally override the kerbside-proxy wheel when building
images. This patch therefore exposes such an override mechanism.

Signed-off-by: Michael Still <mikal@stillhq.com>

revisions.message:
Pass identity credentials to cinder-volume snap

Online volume extends require cinder-volume to notify nova through the
os-server-external-events API. That call needs service credentials in
the [nova] section of cinder.conf, but the charm only forwarded
project-id/user-id to the snap, so the section renders with no auth
options and every online extend fails with:

  keystoneauth1.exceptions.http.BadRequest: Expecting to find domain in
  project. (HTTP 400)

This leaves guests seeing the old disk size.

This change forwards the credentials already available on the
identity-credentials relation to the snap's identity.* configuration
keys, following the same pattern as the openstack-hypervisor charm.
The snap renders these into [nova] as password auth.

Depends on the cinder-volume snap change adding the identity namespace:
https://github.com/canonical/snap-cinder-volume/pull/92

Closes-Bug: #2156802
Change-Id: I1f600abd8f8d2b115573eda88f232a77184e46f5
Signed-off-by: Satya Jhaveri <satya.jhaveri@canonical.com>
(cherry picked from commit 0ac9414c6fdef2b4942a40e5530c94e6d714597b)

subject: Pass identity credentials to cinder-volume snap

etcd: point kube-apiserver at the fixed cluster and keep it correct

The control plane has to reach every member of the cluster, not only
the floating one, so sysinv builds the kube-apiserver --etcd-servers
list from the members that actually exist and applies it without
rebuilding the control plane.

Cluster membership is derived from the cluster itself rather than from
inventory records. Deployment Manager creates controller-1's inventory
record from the deployment config before the machine is installed, so
_get_etcd_cluster_endpoints() now asks etcd directly via
get_cluster_members() rather than relying on a NodeNotFound guard.

The HAProxy backend list is gated on provisioning state: a host
reaches PROVISIONED only once it has been installed and configured.
_get_apiserver_addresses() publishes the provisioned set as
platform::kubernetes::params::apiserver_addresses.

The simplex-to-duplex conversion changes membership, so the conductor
applies the conversion manifest when the system mode changes and
reconciles the endpoint list once the conversion has run.

create-etcd-certs: Add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs

Add cluster-host unit addresses (controller-0, controller-1) to the
subject_alt_name field of etcd-server and apiserver-etcd-client CSRs
generated during bootstrap. This ensures etcd mTLS works on per-controller
addresses when etcd runs as a multi-member cluster.

This prepares the certificates for the Active+Active kube-apiserver
architecture where etcd runs as a 3-member
Raft cluster with fixed members bound to per-controller cluster-host
addresses.

SANs after this change:
- IP: cluster_floating_address (VIP)
- IP: controller_0_cluster_host (unit address)
- IP: controller_1_cluster_host (unit address)
- IP: 127.0.0.1 (loopback)

PASS: etcd accepts certificate with expanded SAN set

PASS: Validated on live AIO-DX VLM lab (192.168.206.1/2/3)

loopback to the subject_alt_name field of etcd-server and

- IP: controller_0_cluster_host (unit address)
- IP: controller_1_cluster_host (unit address, DX only)
- IP: 127.0.0.1 (IPv4 loopback)
- IP: ::1 (IPv6 loopback)

ansible: Bootstrap and restore simplex with etcd-fixed

As part of the etcd architecture redesign, the source of truth for the
etcd cluster is moving from the DRBD-backed floating member to the local
disk fixed-0 member on controller-0.

For simplex deployments, the SM-managed floating etcd instance will no
longer exist. This commit updates the Ansible playbooks to also target
the etcd-fixed systemd service when stopping or starting etcd, ensuring
that both standalone (simplex) and floating (duplex) instances are
appropriately handled during bringup and restore operations.

In addition, it sets etcd_endpoint to controller-0 cluster-host
address for simplex since the floating IP is not used for etcd.

etcd: add certificate SANs and update backup/restore for fixed member

Two related pieces of the fixed-bootstraps-first etcd work that share
files, kept together so they do not collide in review.

Certificate SANs. The etcd cluster on duplex and standard systems runs a
fixed member on each controller, bound to that controller's cluster-host
unit address, alongside the floating member. All members share a single
certificate, so it must carry every address a member can be reached on or
the mTLS handshake fails. Extend the SAN list generated at bootstrap from
{floating, IPv4 loopback} to {floating, controller-0 unit, controller-1
unit, IPv4 loopback, IPv6 loopback}, taking the unit addresses from the
facts validate-config already computes. Those collapse to the floating
address on simplex, and unique() then drops the duplicate so a simplex
certificate carries only addresses that exist.

Backup and restore. Back up from the fixed member endpoints rather than
the floating address, and expose the controller-0 fixed address as its own
fact for callers that need a single authoritative endpoint. Restore the
snapshot into the fixed-0 data directory, which becomes the cluster seed;
the floating member is added later, at controller-0 unlock.

The restore must supply cluster membership explicitly. etcd validates that
--name appears in --initial-cluster, and the built-in default
("default=http://localhost:2380") does not contain fixed-0, so without
--initial-cluster, --initial-cluster-token and
--initial-advertise-peer-urls the restore fails outright:

  Error: couldn't find local name "fixed-0" in the initial cluster
  configuration

The token and peer URL are matched to what puppet writes to
/etc/default/etcd-fixed so the member starts against the restored data.
--mark-compacted and --bump-revision are applied on the etcdutl path only;
they were added to etcdutl in etcd 3.5.9 and etcdctl does not accept them.

Also stop etcd-fixed alongside the floating instance when bootstrap tears
services down for a replay. Neither stop may fail the play, since the
floating instance does not exist on simplex and etcd-fixed may be absent
on an older configuration.

PASS: simplex SAN list collapses to floating, 127.0.0.1 and ::1

      (26 MB, 2124 keys, revision 31299)

Format the etcd endpoint list without the ipwrap filter. The previous
form passed the filter name to map(), which resolves only built-in
filter names, so 'community.general.ipwrap' failed to resolve and the
backup aborted at the etcd snapshot stage on Trixie:

  Format etcd endpoints with proper IPv6 wrapping (Trixie)
  The filter plugin 'ansible.builtin.map' failed:
  No filter named 'community.general.ipwrap'.

The Bullseye branch had the same defect for the same reason; it was
simply not exercised on a Trixie system. Bracket the addresses with
regex_replace instead, which is a built-in and therefore resolvable
through map(). This also matches the reasoning already recorded on the
restore path, where the filter is avoided because it lives in a
different collection on Bullseye and Trixie, and lets the two
distro-specific tasks collapse into one.

Verified on an AIO-DX system that the formatting is correct for both
address families:
  192.168.206.2,192.168.206.3 -> 192.168.206.2:2379,https://192.168.206.3
  fd01::2,fd01::3             -> [fd01::2]:2379,https://[fd01::3]

Five additions bring this to the High Level Design, section 9.

Backup addresses the fixed members on their cluster-host unit addresses rather
than the floating address, because the fixed members are the authoritative
local-disk copies and are present on every system type. etcdctl rejects more
than one endpoint for a snapshot on the count alone, before reachability is
considered, so the endpoints are tried one at a time and the first that answers
is used; a partial file from a failed attempt is removed before the next, and
only the failure of every endpoint is fatal. That is what lets a backup succeed
with one fixed member down.

The cluster membership is now recorded alongside the snapshot, each member name
and peer URL in machine-readable form. The restore rebuilds the cluster rather
than restoring it, and compares the recorded topology against the system it is
restoring onto, so that a restore onto a differently sized or differently
addressed system is identified before any member starts.

The restored member's name is read from /etc/default/etcd-fixed rather than
assumed. The environment file and the restore target must name the same
directory: snapshot restore creates whatever directory it is given, so a
mismatch is not reported -- the database ends up somewhere etcd never opens and
the member starts as an empty single-member cluster instead of failing. On
simplex there is no peer to replicate from, so the data would be lost with no
error raised anywhere in the procedure. The two are now compared and a mismatch
fails loudly. fixed-N naming applies only to systems with more than one
controller, so it cannot be assumed here.

The restored member is rendered with ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE=new, the only
use of new outside bootstrap. The restored data carries the membership of the
cluster that was backed up, which no longer exists; left in place the member
starts expecting peers that are gone and waits for a quorum that can never
form.

The restore then verifies the result before any other member rejoins: exactly
one member, and no address belonging to the cluster that was backed up. A
member that came up retaining the prior membership believes in peers that no
longer exist, and there is no recovery short of wiping the data directory and
restoring again, so this is checked while wiping is still cheap.

Addresses are formatted for URL use through a shared pattern that brackets an
IPv6 literal per RFC 2732, leaves IPv4 unchanged, and leaves an already
bracketed literal alone rather than nesting brackets. An unbracketed IPv4
address is a valid host:port, so this defect class is invisible on IPv4 and
fires only on IPv6.

with the backup failing and no archive written. The fixed endpoint now
falls back to the floating address, which is the same address the fixed
member binds on that system type.

Drop the ETCDCTL_API environment block. etcd 3.6 no longer reads it and
logs "unrecognized environment variable" on every invocation.

Test-Plan: WRCPPV-11147

The etcd membership record is now actually archived. It was generated and
guarded by a hard failure task, but omitted from final_backup_targets, so tar
never picked it up and the file was discarded with the ansible temp directory.
A stock backup produced a tarball containing only etcd-snapshot.db and
etcd-binary-version; with the file listed the tarball carries
etcd-members.json recording every member. Reproduced on both duplex and
simplex, so the omission was topology-independent.

The surrounding comments claimed the restore compares the recorded topology
against the system being restored onto. It does not. The record is archived
for forensics -- what the cluster looked like at backup time, which a support
bundle otherwise cannot answer. A useful comparison would have to be against
the target's configured topology, since a duplex backup records three members
while the restore target is a freshly installed controller-0 with exactly one;
a recorded-versus-live check would reject every valid duplex restore. That is
left as follow-up rather than shipped half-understood, and the comments now say

revisions.message:
playbookconfig: Clean stale etcd state during platform restore

During restore, prepare for automatic etcd 3-member cluster
re-formation by removing stale fixed-member state.

Restore changes (restore-etcd role, duplex only):
- Remove /opt/etcd-fixed/db directory containing stale fixed-member
  data so fresh learner-sync starts clean after restore.
- Remove /etc/platform/.initial_etcd_cluster_config_complete marker
  so the conductor re-runs cluster formation on next start.

Re-formation flow after restore:
- Floating etcd restored from snapshot (existing mechanism).
- Conductor starts, sees no marker, spawns cluster formation.
- Fixed members added as learners, sync from floating, promote.
- Marker re-written -- 3-member cluster operational.
- No manual intervention or etcd commands required.

No backup-side changes needed -- the etcd snapshot already captures
all committed Raft data via the existing etcdctl snapshot mechanism.

Test Plan:
- AIO-DX: backup, restore, verify 3-member cluster re-forms
- AIO-DX: verify data written before backup readable after restore
- AIO-DX: verify no manual etcd commands needed by operator

sysinv: Add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs on renewal

This is a follow-up to the review "create-etcd-certs: Add controller
unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs" [1], which adds the SANs during
bootstrap. This commit handles the certificate renewal path.

Add DB-backed resolution of cluster-host unit addresses for etcd
certificate renewal. The renewed apiserver-etcd-client and etcd-server
certificates now include SANs for the floating IP, both controller
unit IPs, and loopback. Falls back to floating+1/+2 if the DB is
unreachable.

This prepares the certificates for the Active+Active kube-apiserver
architecture where etcd runs as a 3-member Raft cluster with fixed

sysinv: add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs on renewal

This is the renewal counterpart to the bootstrap change "etcd: add
certificate SANs and update backup/restore for fixed member". Bootstrap
generates the etcd certificates with SANs for the floating address, both
controller cluster-host unit addresses and the loopbacks;
kube-cert-rotation.sh must regenerate them with the same set, or the fixed
etcd members become unreachable over mTLS after the first renewal.

Resolve the cluster-host unit addresses by parsing /etc/hosts, where puppet
(via sysinv/puppet/platform.py) writes a controller-X-cluster-host entry on
both controllers. This works identically on the active and the standby
controller, with no dependency on DRBD or PostgreSQL, which matters because
renewal can run on either. If an entry is missing, fall back to deriving the
address from the floating address and log a warning.

The renewed apiserver-etcd-client and etcd-server certificates then carry
IP.1=floating, IP.2=controller-0 unit, IP.3=controller-1 unit,
IP.4=127.0.0.1 and IP.5=::1 -- the same set bootstrap produces.

revisions.message:
sysinv: Add etcd cluster lifecycle management for duplex

In duplex systems, add conductor methods for managing the etcd cluster
through system lifecycle operations (migration, upgrade, rolling
restart).

Migration support (SX-to-DX):
- add_duplex_fixed_etcd_peers() converts standalone floating etcd to a
  3-member cluster by adding controller-0 and controller-1 as learners,
  waiting for replication sync, then promoting to full voters.
  Fully idempotent with marker file guard to prevent re-execution.

Pre-upgrade health gate:
- _validate_etcd_cluster_before_upgrade() queries all etcd members and
  blocks upgrade if any member is unreachable or unhealthy.
- _check_etcd_cluster_health() added to the system upgrade health check
  in common/health.py so the platform reports etcd issues alongside
  other upgrade blockers.

Rolling upgrade quorum safeguard:
- validate_etcd_rolling_upgrade_safe() ensures removing one member for
  binary upgrade will not break cluster consensus. Verifies all other
  members are healthy before proceeding.
- validate_etcd_member_rejoined_after_upgrade() waits for the upgraded
  member to rejoin the cluster and report healthy before the next host
  is upgraded.

Test Plan:
- AIO-DX: verify SX-to-DX migration creates 3-member cluster
- AIO-DX: verify upgrade blocked when etcd member is down
- AIO-DX: verify rolling upgrade maintains quorum throughout

In duplex systems, add conductor methods for managing the etcd cluster
through system lifecycle operations (migration, upgrade, rolling
restart).

Migration support (SX-to-DX):
- add_duplex_fixed_etcd_peers() converts standalone floating etcd to a
  3-member cluster by adding controller-0 and controller-1 as learners,
  waiting for replication sync, then promoting to full voters.
  Fully idempotent with marker file guard to prevent re-execution.

Pre-upgrade health gate:
- _validate_etcd_cluster_before_upgrade() queries all etcd members and
  blocks upgrade if any member is unreachable or unhealthy.
- _check_etcd_cluster_health() added to the system upgrade health check
  in common/health.py so the platform reports etcd issues alongside
  other upgrade blockers.

Rolling upgrade quorum safeguard:
- validate_etcd_rolling_upgrade_safe() ensures removing one member for
  binary upgrade will not break cluster consensus. Verifies all other
  members are healthy before proceeding.
- validate_etcd_member_rejoined_after_upgrade() waits for the upgraded
  member to rejoin the cluster and report healthy before the next host
  is upgraded.

- AIO-DX: verify SX-to-DX migration creates 3-member cluster
- AIO-DX: verify upgrade blocked when etcd member is down

revisions.message:
sysinv: Add periodic etcd cluster health audit with alarm

Add a management-affecting alarm that fires when the etcd cluster
drops below full 3-member quorum, enabling the VIM upgrade strategy
to automatically pause rolling upgrades until quorum is restored.

Periodic audit:
- _audit_etcd_cluster_health() runs every 60 seconds on duplex
  systems once the 3-member cluster has been formed.
- Queries each etcd member via get_members/is_member_healthy.
- Raises FM_ALARM_ID_ETCD_CLUSTER_DEGRADED (850.003, major,
  mgmt_affecting=True) when any member is unhealthy.
- Clears automatically when all members are healthy voters.

Alarm helper:
- _update_etcd_cluster_alarm() sets or clears the alarm using the
  same pattern as _update_k8s_cluster_alarm.
- Entity instance: k8s=etcd-cluster-health.

VIM integration (no nfv change needed):
- WaitDataSyncStep blocks until mgmt-affecting alarms clear.
- Pre-lock QueryAlarmsStep blocks if alarm is active.
- This prevents locking the next controller during rolling upgrade
  until the etcd member has rejoined as a healthy voter.

Test Plan:
- AIO-DX: stop one etcd member, verify alarm raised within 60s
- AIO-DX: restart member, verify alarm clears automatically
- AIO-DX: verify simplex systems are correctly skipped

puppet: Verify floating etcd member identity across SWACT

On AIO-DX the floating etcd member (stable name 'controller') is
SM-managed and DRBD-backed: on SWACT the cluster-host floating IP
and the member data directory move to the newly-active controller
and the service restarts there. Add a post-start verification hook
for this floating member:

- etcd_floating_member.py: after each etcd (re)start, confirm the
  'controller' member is still registered in the cluster, repair
  its advertised peer URLs via 'member update' if they no longer
  match ETCD_INITIAL_ADVERTISE_PEER_URLS from /etc/default/etcd,
  and wait for the local client endpoint to report healthy. The
  script is idempotent and a no-op on a healthy cluster.
- etcd-override.conf.erb: invoke the script via 'ExecStartPost=-'
  so a verification failure is logged but never blocks the etcd
  service itself from starting.
- etcd.pp: install the script as /opt/platform/bin/etcd-floating-member
  from platform::etcd::setup.

Both the bullseye and trixie puppet trees are updated identically.

This change covers the floating member behaviour across SWACT only.
The fixed-member infrastructure that earlier patchsets of this review
carried (etcd-instance unit/env templates and membership management)
is owned by https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/stx-puppet/+/995017
and has been dropped from this review to avoid overlap.

Test plan:
PASS: python3 -m py_compile etcd_floating_member.py
PASS: bootstrap AIO-DX, verify etcd starts and the hook logs
      'Floating member 'controller' verified healthy'
PASS: SWACT, verify the floating member restarts on the new active
      controller with current peer URLs and healthy endpoint

References: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/ansible-playbooks/+/994873
References: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/config/+/994874

DNM: BGP job: set min_compute_nodes to enable DifferentHostFilter

The BGP multinode job has two compute nodes but tempest's
min_compute_nodes defaults to 1, so tests that use
DifferentHostFilter to schedule VMs on separate computes
silently skip the cross-node placement.  Set it to 2 so
the FIP-from-external-network-VM test (and any future
multinode-aware test) actually exercises cross-compute
connectivity.

revisions.message:
kubernetes: enable Active+Active kube-apiserver load balancing

In duplex systems, configure the HAProxy internal backend
(k8s-backend-internal) to load-balance across both controllers'
kube-apiserver instances using round-robin scheduling.

Health checking uses the /readyz endpoint over TLS to detect
application-level failures and remove unhealthy instances from
rotation before the TCP connection drops, reducing failover
impact for internal cluster traffic.

Tuning: inter 2s fall 2 rise 1 for carrier-grade failover
latency (~4s worst case detection).

Simplex mode is unchanged (single backend server, TCP check only).

Test Plan:
PASS: Bootstrap completes successfully with HAProxy load-balancing enabled
PASS: HAProxy correctly routes /readyz checks to both controllers
PASS: No disruption to existing single-node simplex cluster

Story: 2010302
Task: 51206

Fix TLS leaf certificate renewal fallback

Migrate sunbeam TLS requirers from the deprecated tls-certificates
interface library to charmlibs.interfaces.tls_certificates and wire
update-status as a refresh event.

This gives charms a periodic renewal safety net when secret-expired does
not complete, preventing leaf certificates from remaining expired until
workloads fail after restart.

Fix TLS leaf certificate renewal fallback

Migrate sunbeam TLS requirers from the deprecated tls-certificates
interface library to charmlibs.interfaces.tls_certificates and wire
update-status as a refresh event.

This gives charms a periodic renewal safety net when secret-expired does
not complete, preventing leaf certificates from remaining expired until
workloads fail after restart.

The refresh may emit certificate-available events when the certificate
material has not changed. Persist certificate bundle fingerprints and
skip duplicate events to avoid unnecessary charm reconciliation and
workload service restarts.

Only record a fingerprint after configure_charm completes successfully,
so failures handled by the charm guard remain eligible for retry. Prevent
synchronous certificate callbacks from re-entering reconciliation while
certificates are being synchronized.

Closes-Bug: #2159609
Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/sunbeam-charms/+/1000804

Only record a fingerprint after configure_charm completes successfully,

sysinv: Add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs on renewal

Add resolution of cluster-host unit addresses from /etc/hosts for etcd
certificate renewal. Puppet (via sysinv/puppet/platform.py) populates
/etc/hosts with controller-X-cluster-host entries on both controllers,
making this approach reliable on both active and standby without any
DRBD/PostgreSQL dependency.

The renewed apiserver-etcd-client and etcd-server certificates now
include SANs for the floating IP, both controller unit IPs, IPv4
loopback, and IPv6 loopback.

Changes:
- get_cluster_host_unit_ip(): resolves unit address by parsing
  /etc/hosts via awk. Falls back to floating+N arithmetic if entry
  is missing.
- SANs: IP.1=floating, IP.2=ctrl-0, IP.3=ctrl-1, IP.4=127.0.0.1,
  IP.5=::1
- Works identically on active and standby controllers (no DB needed)
- IPv4 and IPv6 compatible

Test Plan:
PASS: kube-cert-rotation.sh resolves unit IPs from /etc/hosts
PASS: Fallback logic (floating+N) produces correct IPs when missing
PASS: Generated cert contains all 5 SANs
PASS: etcd accepts renewed cert without service disruption

Upgrade Calico manifest before Tigera operator migration

The Tigera operator migration only supports auto-detection of network
configuration from the same Calico version manifests. During k8s
upgrades, StarlingX transitions from an older manifest-based Calico
directly to the operator model, which is a cross-version migration
not supported by the operator's auto-detection.

Add an intermediate step to apply the matching Calico manifest before
deploying the Tigera operator. This ensures calico-node is running
the same version as the operator expects, enabling proper
auto-detection of nodeAddressAutodetection, ipPools, and other
network settings during migration.

Test Plan:

- PASS: K8s upgrade from v1.32.2 to v1.35.2 on AIO-DX
- PASS: calico-node Running after migration (no CrashLoopBackOff)
- PASS: Operator auto-detects network config from manifest
- PASS: globalnetworkpolicies accessible post-upgrade

revisions.message:
Allow shrinking a segment range to an allocated boundary

Updating a network segment range to reduce its minimum or maximum was
rejected as referenced by a tenant network even when every allocated
segment still fell within the requested new range. The guard against
stranding allocated segments used inclusive comparisons (>= and <=),
so a new boundary that landed exactly on the lowest or highest
allocated segment was wrongly treated as impacting them.

Use strict comparisons so the update is only blocked when the new
minimum rises above the lowest allocated segment or the new maximum
drops below the highest allocated segment.

Closes-Bug: #2161678
Assisted-By: Claude Opus 4.8
Change-Id: Ibc51c722669f3ea9b16d6821554d92fcb5f924c3
Signed-off-by: Doug Goldstein <cardoe@cardoe.com>

Fix envoy gateway pod failure on IPv6-only during k8s upgrade

Add IPv6-only EnvoyProxy configuration during k8s networking upgrade.
Creates a custom EnvoyProxy CR with admin address bound to all
interfaces and patches the GatewayAPI CR to reference it.

This complements the ansible-playbooks fix for fresh install by
covering the k8s upgrade path via sysinv conductor.

The fix is conditional and only applies to IPv6-only systems.

 - Verified pod comes up 2/2 on IPv6-only system
 - Verified pod survives Tigera operator restart
 - Verified pod survives lock/unlock

revisions.message:
Avoid rotation of manually created cinder-backups

Existing rotation logic for cinder-backup does not account for
manually created backups. This means, that if user has created a backup
for the same volume, that is managed by freezer - this backup
will be rotated by freezer.

In order to fix the issue, we leverage new /backups PATH method,
where backup record is being created, so we have backup UUID.
This uuid is written down to cinder-backup metadata, while
cinder-backup UUID is pushed to the /backups through PATCH, as well as
the status update.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/freezer-api/+/998519
Change-Id: I30f2c8ec6444c9e00a33c770eb269f53fd41d114
Signed-off-by: Dmitriy Rabotyagov <dmitriy.rabotyagov@cleura.com>

Avoid rotation of manually created cinder-backups

Existing rotation logic for cinder-backup does not account for
manually created backups. This means, that if user has created a backup
for the same volume, that is managed by freezer - this backup
will be rotated by freezer.

In order to fix the issue, we leverage new /backups PATH method,
where backup record is being created, so we have backup UUID.
This uuid is written down to cinder-backup metadata, while
cinder-backup UUID is pushed to the /backups through PATCH, as well as
the status update.

revisions.message:
Reset N3000 FPGAs using the host OPAE rsu tool

The N3000 reset was driven through the starlingx/n3000-opae container
image ("ctr -n=k8s.io run --rm --privileged ... rsu bmcimg"), so the
reset at boot depended on containerd being up and on the image being
present in, or pullable into, containerd.

Both preconditions are gone now:

 - the OPAE SDK 2.14.0 is built and shipped as host packages (opae,
   opae-devel, opae-extra-tools), so /usr/bin/rsu is installed on the
   platform;

 - the in-tree intel-m10bmc-sec-update driver exposes the
   control/available_images and control/image_load sysfs nodes, which
   is the interface rsu drives to reload an image. On an N3000
   available_images reports "bmc_factory bmc_user retimer_fw".

Invoke rsu directly on the host and drop the container path entirely:
image discovery and pull (n3000_img_accessible), the containerd
snapshot/container cleanup (cleanup_resource) and the image pinning
performed after a successful reset are no longer required.

This also supersedes the workaround from "Skip N3000 OPAE reset when
in-tree DFL stack manages the device". With the control nodes in place
the reset is functional on kernels where /sys/class/fpga_sec_mgr has
been removed, so it must no longer be skipped there; the in-tree stack
detection is removed.

The retimer reload is switched over as well. It used to write 1 to
pkvl/eeprom_load and poll pkvl/eeprom_update_status for 0x1111, both
provided by the out-of-tree intel-opae-fpga module, which is not built
for Debian trixie. Under the in-tree DFL stack the card enumerates as
  <pci_addr>/fpga_region/region0/dfl-fme.0/dfl_dev.0/
      subdev_spi_altera.2.auto/spi_master/spi1/spi1.0/
          n3000bmc-sec-update.5.auto
so the FME and SPI glob patterns matched nothing, no pkvl node exists
anywhere under /sys, and the retimer step could only ever fail.

Use "rsu retimer" instead, which drives control/image_load with the
retimer_fw key word. The eeprom_update_status check has no equivalent
in the in-tree ABI and is dropped in favour of the rsu exit status. The
now unused sysfs path constants and get_n3000_sysfs_file() are removed.

rsu removes the parent bridge from the PCIe bus and rescans it, which
can renumber the bus: on an AIO-SX the card moved from 0000:b3:00.0 to
0000:b2:00.0 across a reset. The retimer step therefore re-queries the
device list before the second reset rather than reusing the addresses
it started from, which no longer necessarily identify the card.

When /usr/bin/rsu is not installed the reset now fails without creating
the .sysinv_n3000_reset flag, so it is retried on the next attempt,
matching the previous behaviour when the OPAE image was not ready.

Test Plan:
  PASS: AIO-SX with an N3000 on a kernel without /sys/class/fpga_sec_mgr,
        opae 2.14.0 installed from the host packages: "rsu bmc" and
        "rsu retimer" each report "RSU operation complete".
  PASS: sysinv-reset-n3000-fpgas with .sysinv_n3000_retimer set runs
        "rsu bmcimg" on 0000:b2:00.0, then "rsu retimer", then a second
        "rsu bmcimg", logs "Done resetting N3000 FPGAs." and exits 0.
        No containerd image or container is involved.
  PASS: rsu re-enumerates the bus after each operation; the card is
        found again by the device query preceding the second reset.
  PASS: .sysinv_n3000_reset is created and .sysinv_n3000_retimer is
        removed once the sequence completes.
  PASS: A second sysinv-reset-n3000-fpgas exits 0 immediately, without
        invoking rsu, on the strength of the .sysinv_n3000_reset flag.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/config/+/996132

revisions.message:
Update N3000 device images with the host OPAE fpgasupdate tool

Writing a device image to an N3000 ran fpgasupdate inside the
starlingx/n3000-opae container, with the image cache bind mounted at
/mnt/images. Now that the OPAE SDK is shipped as host packages,
/usr/bin/fpgasupdate is available on the platform, so run it directly
on the cached image file.

This drops the last two consumers of the container image:

 - cleanup_container(), which removed an n3000-opae container left
   behind when the host rebooted during a device update. Without a
   container there is nothing to clean up.

 - set_cgroup_cpuset(), which created /sys/fs/cgroup/cpuset/platform
   and seeded it from PLATFORM_CPU_LIST so the container could be
   started with "--cgroup platform". fpgasupdate is now a child of
   sysinv-agent and inherits its cgroup, and the cgroup v1 path this
   wrote to is not where Debian trixie places the platform cpuset.

The OPAE_IMG and OPAE_IMG_PREV constants have no remaining users and
are removed with them.

The locale workaround is kept, since the OPAE python tools still fail
on a non UTF-8 locale, but it is passed through the environment of the
child process rather than as container arguments, and it now asks for
C.UTF-8: en_US.UTF-8 has to be generated to exist, which was fine
inside the container image but is not guaranteed on the platform.

fpgasupdate is not on the PATH of a system without the opae package,
where subprocess raises FileNotFoundError rather than the
CalledProcessError this code handles, so its presence is checked up
front and reported as a SysinvException.

Test Plan:
  PASS: fpgasupdate 1.4.6 is installed at /usr/bin/fpgasupdate on an
        AIO-SX carrying the opae host packages, and takes the
        "-y --log-level debug <file> <bdf>" form used here.

revisions.message:
Add puppet exec to clear federation deferred flag

Change-Id: Ieac8ef3722e6300026473d0ec219da0c46d6dc8f
Signed-off-by: Felipe Vasconcelos <Felipe.Vasconcelos@windriver.com>

Add puppet exec to clear federation deferred flag

After the keystone federation class applies (or cleans up) resources,
remove the .federation_config_required flag file. This ensures the
conductor periodic audit does not re-trigger puppet on the next cycle.

Placing the removal in puppet (rather than sysinv) provides natural
retry: if puppet fails at any earlier step, the flag remains and the
conductor retries on the next audit interval (~60s).

The exec is added to both the 'if $oidc_issuer_url' branch (after
resource creation) and the 'else' branch (after resource cleanup)
in both bullseye and trixie subtrees.

Test plan:
PASS: Upgrade 26.03 to 26.09, verify flag removed after puppet applies
federation resources (conductor log shows single trigger, no repeated
attempts).
PASS: Simulate puppet failure (e.g. keystone unresponsive), verify flag
persists and conductor retries on next cycle.
PASS: Fresh install, verify flag created by manifest/post and removed
after puppet runs via operation/post path.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/config/+/995395

bgp: Configure OVN resources based on the leak_routes attribute

The patch introduces two commands: Leak and Unleak.

The Leak command connects the bgp-lr-main router with an unused
connection to the leaked LS, if it's the first subnet from
the LS. Then implements a static route on the
bgp-lr-main to route the traffic for the leaked subnet.

Unleak removes the associated static route and if it's the last subnet
on the LS, removes the connection between the bgp-lr-main and the LS.

The OVN resources are also torn down if the subnet is detached from
the Neutron router connected to an external network.

revisions.message:
Add the track attributions API

Lets a subject see and govern who they are recorded as having been
aboard with, and gives vehicle managers the manual escape hatch.

The authorization split is the point of the whole design, so it is
narrow on purpose.  A subject sets the public flag on their own
association and nobody else's -- not even the vehicle's owner, who
governs the track's visibility instead.  A manager who wants a track
private changes the track, not someone else's association with it.

A coalesced group association is not directly settable at all: its
value is the conjunction of its members' own choices, so allowing it to
be set would let one member publish another's presence.  That returns a
409 explaining it is derived.

Changing a flag re-resolves the track, because a coalesced group's
derived value depends on its members' effective values and would
otherwise sit stale until something else touched the vehicle.

Manual attributions cover "the resolver missed it" or "the guest never
checked in", and only vehicle managers can add or remove them.  Removal
is refused for resolver-owned rows: those are derived facts, withdrawn
by the resolver when their check-ins stop overlapping, not by hand.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_0138FLC7QRSZEavCnFWp3t3r
Change-Id: I921590cd55cceb6561f981fd241dc82b13c2bfc1

upsert() loops now instead of trusting the row it read.  It decides
from a snapshot and then writes by id, and withdraw_manual() deletes a
manual-only record outright: a withdrawal landing in that window left
the conditional update matching nothing, and returning None there
threw away the automatic support the resolver had just computed -- the
association would disappear from the subject's map until some later
run happened to recreate it.  A vanished row now sends it back for a
fresh read, where it inserts instead; a concurrent insert of the same
(track_id, subject_id) pair is caught on the unique index and folded
into the winner the same way.  This is the pattern withdraw_manual
already uses, and the write half is split into _write_upsert() so the
retry reads as one decision per attempt.

revisions.message:
Read N3000 FPGA info from in-tree DFL drivers

The sysinv FPGA agent read the N3000 device information from the sysfs
layout exposed by the old out-of-tree OPAE drivers (intel-fpga-fme,
spi-altera, ifpga_sec_mgr). With the move to the in-tree DFL drivers
those paths no longer exist, so the agent reported empty values for the
BMC versions, root hash, cancelled CSKs, boot page and retimer versions.

Update the agent to the in-tree sysfs layout:
- Match a card through its intel-m10bmc-sec-update platform device by
  resolving the PCI address in the device's realpath, instead of walking
  the FME/SPI directories under the PCI device.
- Read the root hash and cancelled CSKs from the secure update device
  (security/sr_root_entry_hash, security/sr_canceled_csks) and the BMC
  firmware/build versions from its parent m10-bmc device.
- Read the boot page and the C827 retimer versions from "fpgainfo fme"
  and "fpgainfo phy", since the in-tree drivers do not export them
  through sysfs. Run each fpgainfo subcommand once per device and parse
  its labelled output.

The reported FPGA information is unchanged from the operator's point of
view; only the source of the data changes.

Test Plan:
  PASS: N3000 detected and inventoried on a host with the in-tree DFL
        drivers; BMC versions, root hash, cancelled CSKs, boot page and
        retimer A/B versions populated in "system host-device-list".
  PASS: Values match those reported by the fpgainfo tool.

etcd: Redesign bootstrap to use fixed member on local disk

This commit redesigns the etcd-fixed architecture to solve the
simplex deadlock issue. It removes all SM management of etcd-fixed
and etcd is managed exclusively by systemd.

During bootstrap (when cluster_host network is not fully separated
or its hieradata is incomplete), etcd-fixed falls back to using
the mgmt network IP addresses for binding.

The python script etcd_fixed_membership.py is heavily enhanced
with idempotency, learner retry, and promotion logic to safely
transition simplex floating -> fixed-0 without timeout failures.

revisions.message:
Add per-provider SSO logout redirect support

Enable Horizon to redirect to the correct SSO logout URL when multiple
authentication methods are configured. This addresses a critical gap
where operators using Keystone + OIDC + SAML2 (or any combination)
cannot configure per-provider logout URLs.

Current behavior:
- WEBSSO_DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LOGOUT only supports single-provider deployments
- Users logged in via SSO remain logged in after "logging out" of Horizon
- This causes security audit failures and confusing UX

This change introduces WEBSSO_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_MAPPING, a dictionary that
maps authentication method identifiers (from WEBSSO_CHOICES or
WEBSSO_IDP_MAPPING) to their respective logout URLs. The logout view
reads the user's session auth_type (already tracked during login) to
determine which logout URL to redirect to.

Example configuration:
    WEBSSO_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_MAPPING = {
        "oidc": "https://idp.example.com/oidc/logout",
        "saml2": "https://idp.example.com/saml2/logout",
    }

Changes:
- openstack_auth/defaults.py: Add WEBSSO_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_MAPPING setting
- openstack_auth/views.py: Modify logout() to use auth_type mapping
- doc/source/configuration/settings.rst: Document new setting
- releasenotes/notes: Add release note

Backward compatibility: Existing single-provider deployments using
WEBSSO_DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LOGOUT continue to work unchanged.

Related-Bug: OSPRH-25872
Related-Bug: RHOSRFE-300

Add per-provider SSO logout redirect support

This patch extends the WEBSSO_POST_LOGOUT_URL setting to support
multi-provider deployments where different SSO methods require
different logout URLs.

When WEBSSO_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_MAPPING is configured, the logout view
checks the user's auth_type and redirects to the provider-specific
logout URL. If no mapping is found, it falls back to
WEBSSO_POST_LOGOUT_URL (for all SSO users) or the existing
WEBSSO_DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LOGOUT.

Configuration tiers (priority order):
1. WEBSSO_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_MAPPING[auth_type] (most specific)
2. WEBSSO_POST_LOGOUT_URL (all SSO users, from parent patch)
3. WEBSSO_DEFAULT_REDIRECT_LOGOUT (legacy single-provider)

Example multi-provider configuration:
    WEBSSO_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_MAPPING = {
        "oidc": "https://idp.example.com/oidc/logout",
        "saml2": "https://idp.example.com/saml2/logout",
    }

Simple deployments can continue using WEBSSO_POST_LOGOUT_URL without
needing a dictionary.

Changes:
- openstack_auth/defaults.py: Add WEBSSO_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_MAPPING setting
- openstack_auth/views.py: Implement tiered fallback logout redirect
- doc/source/configuration/settings.rst: Document new setting with examples
- releasenotes/notes: Add release note explaining tiered system

Increase DRBD CPU mask size from 32 to 256

Add patch to increase DRBD_CPU_MASK_SIZE from 32 to 256 in
drbd-headers/linux/drbd.h. This removes the 112-core limitation
for platform CPU assignments on hardware with more than 56 physical
cores (112 logical with HT).

The patch is a cherry-pick of upstream LINBIT/drbd-headers commit
5697d9932836d9550bbb6fe7c0cac0a2094e9be9, included in drbd-utils
v9.26.0.

revisions.message:
Validate configuration before instance attachment

Configuration groups can pass Trove's parameter rules while still being
rejected by the database engine. Attaching such a group can leave the
instance with a configuration that the datastore cannot load.

Before attaching a configuration group, validate the requested overrides
in the guest-agent; build a temporary candidate from the current datastore
configuration and run the native parser in an isolated one-shot container
without starting the database daemon.

On validation failure, return the parser error and leave the live
configuration unchanged. On success, continue through the existing
configuration save and apply flow.

Validate configuration groups with datastore engines

Configuration values may pass Trove's static validation rules while still
being rejected by the database engine. Applying such values can prevent the
database from starting.

Validate MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL configuration groups using their native
parsers in an isolated one-shot container. Run validation before attaching a
configuration group to an existing instance and during initial instance
preparation.

For attach requests, return HTTP 422 without changing the live configuration
when validation fails. For instance creation, propagate the parser error so
that the instance enters the ERROR state with the reason available in its
fault information.

revisions.message:
synce plugin: add configurable holdover timer

Extend the collectd synce plugin state machine with a holdover timer
that starts counting when the EEC DPLL enters HOLDOVER. If the source
does not recover before the timer expires, the plugin transitions
from holdover_ql to freerun_ql and escalates the FM alarm from major
to critical.

The timer duration is configurable via the holdover_timer parameter
in instance-monitoring.conf (default: 14400 seconds / 4 hours).
On recovery (DPLL returns to LOCKED) or direct transition to
UNLOCKED/FREERUN, the timer is cancelled.

Also clear stale synce alarms on plugin init, following the same
pattern as the ptp plugin. The ptp plugin explicitly skips synce
alarms during its startup audit, so the synce plugin must handle
its own. This prevents orphaned alarms after collectd restart.

Test Plan:
PASS: GNSS disconnect → HOLDOVER, timer started, alarm major
PASS: Timer expired → QL freerun, alarm escalated to critical
PASS: Recovery after expiry → timer cleared, alarm cleared
PASS: Recovery before expiry → timer cancelled, alarm cleared
PASS: Stale alarm cleared on collectd restart
PASS: Unit tests (12 new: timer paths + stale alarm init)

revisions.message:
EVPN: Create a dummy interface per L3 VNI

OVN implementation assumes that each logical switch associated with a
VNI, i.e., a logical with the option "dynamic-routing-vni", must
also set the options "dynamic-routing-advertisement-ifname",
regardless of whether the logical switch supports Type-2 or Type-5
routes.  (The "advertisement" interface is where OVN monitors for
learned neighbors through EVPN Type-2 routes, so the interface is not
used for EVPN Type-5 routes.)  Without setting the option
"dynamic-routing-advertisement-ifname", OVN continuously logs a warning
about the missing "advertisement" interface.

Related-Bug: #2146617

Mount host /home/sysadmin/ in ptp-notification DaemonSet for custom leapfile path

Add a volume mount for /home/sysadmin/ in the ptp-notification DaemonSet
to support user-configurable leapfile paths in the ts2phc config.

When a sysadmin configures the leapfile to a custom path (e.g.,
/home/sysadmin/leap-seconds.list), the container needs access to that
location. Previously, only /usr/share/zoneinfo/ was mounted, so files
stored elsewhere were inaccessible to the container.

Puppet manages a symlink from /usr/share/zoneinfo/leap-seconds.list to
the user-configured path when it differs from the default location.
This additional mount ensures the symlink target is accessible from
within the container.

Test Plan:
- Configured leapfile in ts2phc config to /home/sysadmin/leap-seconds.list
- Created symlink: /usr/share/zoneinfo/leap-seconds.list -> /home/sysadmin/leap-seconds.list
- Verified symlink resolves correctly from within the ptp-notification container
- Confirmed the container can read the leapfile content through the symlink
- Tested with leapfile at default path (/usr/share/zoneinfo/leap-seconds.list)
  with no symlink and verified it still works as expected
- Verified pod schedules successfully with the new volume mount

Document extraHostPathMounts for auditd file watch rules

The auditd documentation only showed syscall-based audit rules
in the example override file. Users applying file watch rules
(-w /etc/kubernetes/...) had no guidance on how to make the
watched paths visible inside the auditd container, resulting
in 'No such file or directory' errors at rule-load time.

Update the audit.rules override example to include file watch
rules with the corresponding extraHostPathMounts configuration,
and add a note explaining that file watch rules require the
target path to be mounted into the container.

sysinv: Add all controller IPs to etcd certificate SANs on renewal

FR-06: etcd certificates must include Subject Alternative Names for
all cluster-host unit addresses (controller-0, controller-1) in
addition to the floating address and loopback, so that mTLS
connections succeed across all etcd members in the multi-instance
cluster.

Changes to kube-cert-rotation.sh:
- Add get_cluster_host_unit_ip() helper that resolves controller
  unit addresses from /etc/hosts with arithmetic fallback.
- Resolve controller-0 and controller-1 cluster-host addresses
  before cert renewal, with error handling if resolution fails.
- Update apiserver-etcd-client and etcd-server cert SANs to include
  all controller unit IPs, floating IP, IPv4 and IPv6 loopback.

SAN order matches the deployed etcd cert (controller IPs first):
  IP.1=controller-0, IP.2=controller-1, IP.3=floating,
  IP.4=127.0.0.1, IP.5=::1

ansible: Bootstrap and restore simplex with etcd-fixed
As part of the etcd architecture redesign, the source of truth for the
etcd cluster is moving from the DRBD-backed floating member to the local
disk fixed-0 member on controller-0.
For simplex deployments, the SM-managed floating etcd instance will no
longer exist. This commit updates the Ansible playbooks to also target
the etcd-fixed systemd service when stopping or starting etcd, ensuring
that both standalone (simplex) and floating (duplex) instances are
appropriately handled during bringup and restore operations.
In addition, it sets etcd_endpoint to controller-0 cluster-host
address for simplex since the floating IP is not used for etcd.
Story: 2010302
Task: 51206

Depends-On: I30d5c854774da7e3c28d893054b047ef7fce073c
Test-Plan: WRCPPV-11147
Change-Id: I64fe6f146b8ed24232ae7eb8ee5c5d7bc1515b0c
Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

revisions.message:
Add API definitions for port groups

A port group is a reusable collection of ports and port ranges, that can
be referenced by a security group rule instead of a single port or a
single contiguous port range. This adds the API definitions of the three
extensions needed by that feature:

* ``port-group``: the port group resource itself, along with the
  ``add_ports`` and ``remove_ports`` actions. Those actions use ``PUT``,
  following ``add_addresses`` and ``remove_addresses`` of the address
  group API.
* ``security-groups-port-group``: adds the ``port_group_id`` field to the
  security group rules, following the existing
  ``security-groups-remote-address-group`` extension.
* ``rbac-port-group``: shim extension registering the ``port_group``
  object type in the network RBAC framework, so that a port group can be
  shared with other projects the same way an address group is.

The ``ports`` attribute is a list of ``port_range_min`` and
``port_range_max`` pairs, a single port being expressed as a range with
the same minimum and maximum value. The relation between the two values
is not checked by the API definition, it is enforced by the service
plugin.

This only adds the API definitions. The implementation will follow in
neutron.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/neutron-specs/+/987786
Related-Bug: #2147189
Change-Id: I23d82fa48336086211d6b6a7b1c8dfba32a5d9cd

sysinv: Add etcd cluster membership helper functions

Add helper functions to sysinv/common/etcd.py for managing etcd
cluster membership in the multi-instance topology, where the fixed
instance on controller-0 founds the cluster and additional members
(the DRBD-backed floating instance, and the fixed instance on
controller-1) join the running cluster.

Functions added:
- get_members(): list cluster members with raw etcdctl JSON fields
- member_exists(): check membership by name
- add_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member add', returns member ID
- remove_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member remove' by name
- is_endpoint_healthy() / wait_for_endpoint(): endpoint health polling
- get_cluster_health(): returns healthy/total counts and unhealthy names

These are consumed by the conductor for cluster lifecycle operations
(simplex-to-duplex migration, platform upgrade and rollback) and by
the periodic cluster health audit.

Change-Id: Iba595ee8010d466ef0035d96daa50657b797f6a2
Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

sysinv: Add etcd cluster membership helper functions

Add helper functions to sysinv/common/etcd.py for managing etcd
cluster membership in the multi-instance topology, where the fixed
instance on controller-0 founds the cluster and additional members
(the DRBD-backed floating instance, and the fixed instance on
controller-1) join the running cluster.

Functions added:
- get_members(): list cluster members with raw etcdctl JSON fields
- member_exists(): check membership by name
- add_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member add', returns member ID
- remove_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member remove' by name
- is_endpoint_healthy() / wait_for_endpoint(): endpoint health polling
- get_configured_member_count(): expected size for the system mode
- is_voting_member(): whether a member counts towards quorum
- get_cluster_health(): healthy/total counts and degraded member names

Cluster health is accounted for as the high level design requires.
Two points follow from that design and are reflected here:

- Health is measured against the member count the system is
  configured for, not the count currently registered. The two differ
  only while a procedure is deliberately growing or shrinking the
  cluster, and an alarm keyed to the registered count would assert
  continuously through those steps and gate the very operations it
  exists to protect. get_cluster_health() therefore accepts the
  system mode and reports missing members explicitly. The parameter
  is optional, so existing callers keep the previous behaviour.

- A learner is never counted healthy. It replicates the log but does
  not vote, so it cannot keep the cluster available, and etcd refuses
  the health RPC against it in any case. Such a member is reported as
  "<name> (learner)" to distinguish a member that needs promoting
  from one that needs recovering.

These are consumed by the conductor for cluster lifecycle operations
(simplex-to-duplex migration, platform upgrade and rollback) and by
the periodic cluster health audit.

Unit tests cover the configured member count per system mode, voter
and learner classification, and the health accounting for a fully
healthy cluster, a learner member, an unregistered member, an
unreachable member, a member without a client URL, simplex, an empty
member list, and the no-system-mode fallback.

Test-Plan: WRCPPV-11147
Change-Id: Iba595ee8010d466ef0035d96daa50657b797f6a2
Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

sysinv: Add etcd cluster health helpers, audit alarm and upgrade gate

Introduce the etcd cluster health surface used across the
Active+Active control plane work:

* sysinv/common/etcd.py — membership and health helpers
  (get_members, member_exists, add_member, remove_member,
  is_endpoint_healthy, wait_for_endpoint, get_cluster_health)
  with unit coverage.
* conductor/manager.py — periodic _audit_etcd_cluster_health task
  raising the management-affecting 850.003 alarm when the cluster
  is short of its configured member count, clearing once every
  member is a healthy voter again. Audit interval defaults to 60s
  to satisfy the 60-second alarm requirement. Skipped on simplex.
* common/health.py — pre-upgrade gate refusing to start a platform
  upgrade while the etcd cluster is degraded, with unit coverage.

The helpers, the audit and the gate share the same health
evaluation, so they are delivered together; splitting them left
the gate and the audit each depending on an unreviewable subset
of the helpers.

The 850.003 alarm definition is registered separately in
starlingx/fault.

Active+Active control plane work:

* sysinv/common/etcd.py — membership and health helpers
  (get_members, member_exists, add_member, remove_member,
  is_endpoint_healthy, wait_for_endpoint, get_cluster_health)
  with unit coverage.
* conductor/manager.py — periodic _audit_etcd_cluster_health task
  raising the management-affecting 850.003 alarm when the cluster
  is short of its configured member count, clearing once every
  member is a healthy voter again. Audit interval defaults to 60s
  to satisfy the 60-second alarm requirement. Skipped on simplex.
* common/health.py — pre-upgrade gate refusing to start a platform
  upgrade while the etcd cluster is degraded, with unit coverage.

The helpers, the audit and the gate share the same health
evaluation, so they are delivered together; splitting them left
the gate and the audit each depending on an unreviewable subset
of the helpers.

The 850.003 alarm definition is registered separately in
starlingx/fault.

previously used only the loopback endpoint, so when the local member was

  850.003  etcd cluster degraded: 0/3 healthy voting members (degraded: )

Adds ensure_cert_sans(), which regenerates the etcd certificates when
they do not name every member address. A system upgraded from a release
that ran a single DRBD-backed instance carries a certificate whose SANs
name only the floating address and the loopback addresses:

  SAN: IP Address:192.168.206.1, IP Address:127.0.0.1

The fixed instances bind the controller cluster-host addresses, so every
TLS connection to them fails verification:

  x509: certificate is valid for 192.168.206.1, 127.0.0.1,
        not 192.168.206.2

which surfaces as the member never becoming healthy and so never being
promoted, leaving the cluster short of its members with no indication
that a certificate is the cause.

The regenerated certificate is a union with what is already present
rather than a replacement, so the floating address is never dropped --
the caller names the fixed members, and the floating instance is the one
member serving the cluster while the others are being added.

The CA, validity and extension set match kube-cert-rotation.sh, so a
certificate produced here and one produced by the next scheduled rotation
are equivalent. Nothing is done when every address is already covered,
which makes this safe to call on every activate and a no-op on simplex,
where controller-0 cluster-host address and the floating address are the
same and so already present.

served by the FIXED instance, which lists https://127.0.0.1:2379 in its

cluster-host floating address:

  /etc/default/etcd         ETCD_LISTEN_CLIENT_URLS="https://192.168.206.1:2379"
  /etc/default/etcd-fixed   ETCD_LISTEN_CLIENT_URLS="https://192.168.206.2:2379,

  ss -ltnp   127.0.0.1:2379      -> etcd-fixed     (Main PID 5905)

During an upgrade activate the fixed instances are deliberately not started
yet, so nothing answers on loopback and every conductor call failed with
"dial tcp 127.0.0.1:2379: connect: connection refused". The membership audit
then deferred on every pass and the cluster was never completed. The fixed
instance having bound loopback on the previous release is why this went
unnoticed: the operations only appeared to work because an ungated service was
already running.

member's address, in _etcdctl_base() so that all helpers reach the cluster the
same way. ETCD_LOCAL_ENDPOINT remains only as the fallback for when no
cluster-host name resolves, and its comment now records why loopback is not a
general answer.

Tests cover reaching the cluster with nothing on loopback, honouring an
explicit endpoint, never emitting a hostname endpoint, simplex deduplication,
and finding an unstarted learner by peer URL.

boolean so add_member() can report the ID of a member it finds already
registered. member_exists() is a wrapper over it, so the two cannot drift
apart again. _member_id() raises rather than substituting a default, because
the ID is passed to promote_member() and member remove and '0' matches no
member, so a placeholder would turn a missing ID into an operation against
nothing.

members from member_exists(name) with no peer URL, which on the lab let
activate-rollback finish without removing anything. It lives in the change that
adds the audit dispatch rather than here, and is noted there.

and the name-based list returned none.

cluster-host name resolves, and its comment now records why loopback is not a

sysinv: add etcd membership and health helpers

Add the helpers the conductor needs to inspect and change etcd cluster
membership, and an audit that alarms when the cluster is degraded.

common/etcd.py gains membership operations (list, add, promote, remove,
find) and health operations (per-endpoint health, wait-for-endpoint,
whole-cluster health). Three properties of etcd shape the interface:

  - A member is identified by peer URL as well as by name, because etcd
    assigns a name only when the member starts and introduces itself. A
    member registered but not yet started carries an empty name, so a
    name-only lookup reports it absent.

  - Members are registered as learners. Registration changes the quorum
    requirement at the moment it happens rather than when the member
    starts, so registering a voter into a cluster of N voters requires
    (N+1)/2+1 while only N are running. On the smallest clusters that is
    immediately fatal.

  - Endpoints are addresses, not names. The etcd certificates carry IP
    subjectAltNames and no DNS names, so a hostname endpoint fails
    verification against every member.

Endpoints are resolved from the cluster-host names rather than assuming
loopback. Loopback is served by the fixed instance; the floating instance
listens only on the cluster-host floating address, so during an upgrade
activate, when the fixed instances are deliberately not started, nothing
answers on it.

Every etcdctl invocation is bounded by a timeout. These calls otherwise
hang rather than fail, waiting on TLS handshake, name resolution, leader
election and request forwarding, and a hung call in the periodic audit
holds the conductor greenthread for its duration.

health.py reports etcd in the base system health query, so a degraded
cluster is visible to any caller rather than only on the platform upgrade
path. The Kubernetes version upgrade and root CA update paths opt out:
neither changes etcd membership, and gating a root CA update on etcd
health would block the operation needed to recover from an etcd
certificate that no longer matches the cluster.

The conductor audits cluster health periodically and raises alarm 850.003
when the cluster is short of its configured member count, clearing it once
every member is a healthy voter again. Health is measured against the
configured topology rather than the registered membership, so the alarm
does not assert continuously while a procedure is deliberately growing or
shrinking the cluster.

  PASS  simplex: endpoints deduplicate to one address, health (1, 1, [])

Add the helpers the conductor uses to read and change etcd cluster
membership, and report cluster health from a periodic audit that raises
alarm 850.003 when the cluster is short of its configured member count.

Every etcdctl invocation carries etcdctl's own --command-timeout and
--dial-timeout rather than only a wall-clock bound on the subprocess, so
a call is cut short where it can actually be interrupted. Defaults are
5s command and 2s dial, matching the duplex migration script so the two
sources stay aligned; membership changes use 15s because they commit
through raft, and a snapshot save 30s because it streams the keyspace.
The subprocess bound is derived as dial + command + 1s so the two cannot
drift.

Health is measured against the configured topology rather than the
registered membership, so the alarm does not assert continuously while a
procedure is deliberately growing or shrinking the cluster.

Enable fake FPGA program tests in tempest.conf

cyborg-tempest-plugin [1] adds a scenario test

collect: add NUMA topology info to collect_extra

Adds numa.info with the following commands:
- numactl --hardware : NUMA node memory totals and distances
- numastat -m        : per-node free/used memory breakdown
- lstopo ASCII       : per-node topology in text form

Adds the following SVG files to var/extra/:

  numa_topology.svg
    Full-system topology showing all NUMA nodes, CPU sockets,
    cores, threads, L1/L2/L3 caches and memory per node.

  numa_topology_node<N>.svg
    Per-node topology restricted to node N. One file per node
    found under /sys/devices/system/node/. Useful for comparing
    node layouts on asymmetric topologies such as SNC on Intel
    or NPS2/NPS4 on AMD EPYC.

  SVG files can be opened in any web browser.

[stable-only] Set skip-level grenade as voting

setuptools is 59.6.0, which does not have yet the build method
build_meta.prepare_metadata_for_build_editable, but we are using now
newer pbr version (7.0.0) which would use the mentioned method.
