revisions.message:
fix: network segment range update range test was incorrect

The existing test creates a network segment range from 1100 to 1105 and
then creates a network getting segment_id=1100 assigned. It then
attempted to adjust the segment range to 1100 to 1155 and expected this
to throw a Conflict exception. This is incorrect as there is no conflict
and that is a valid range. Updated the existing test to attempt to set
the range to the created network PLUS 1 to 1155. This ensures that the
attempt to adjust the range is to a minimum and maximum combo that
excludes the existing network and should result in a failure. Add a new
test to confirm that the behavior of shrinking a network segment range
to include the created network does in fact work.

Change-Id: I4cf24eab179f58c37af795d0c6fa874f82ae823a
Signed-off-by: Doug Goldstein <cardoe@cardoe.com>

revisions.message:
Harden openstack API workers and DaemonSet waits

Three related exposures found while investigating an application
update that aborted at 95 percent and whose recovery then failed on
cinder.

1. cinder-api ran a single uwsgi process

The chart derives the process count in
cinder/templates/configmap-etc.yaml:

  if empty .Values.conf.cinder_api_uwsgi.uwsgi.processes
    set processes = .Values.conf.cinder.DEFAULT.osapi_volume_workers

The static overrides leave processes empty and pinned
osapi_volume_workers to 1, so the derived value was 1. With one
process a single stalled request blocks every subsequent one,
including the startup probe. The probe then fails, cinder-api
crashloops, the post-upgrade hooks time out and the release fails
with:

  post-upgrade hooks failed: client rate limiter Wait returned an
  error: rate: Wait(n=1) would exceed context deadline

Because placement depends on cinder that failure cascades and stalls
the releases behind it, which aborts an in-progress application
recovery.

2. heat-api and heat-api-cfn had the same exposure

heat/templates/configmap-etc.yaml derives
heat_api_uwsgi.uwsgi.processes and heat_api_cfn_uwsgi.uwsgi.processes
from conf.heat.heat_api.workers and conf.heat.heat_api_cfn.workers in
exactly the same way, and both were pinned to 1. heat also sits in the
dependency graph, so a wedged heat-api stalls the releases behind it.

Raise all three to 2, matching the existing precedent in
glance-static-overrides.yaml which overrides the same upstream default
of 1 to 2. This leaves a second process able to serve probes while one
is stalled. conf.heat.DEFAULT.num_engine_workers is left at 1, it is
not a uwsgi-backed API.

3. clients and gnocchi could stall a release on a DaemonSet rollout

Both ship DaemonSets but had no disableWait, so Flux waits for the
rollout to complete and fails the release on the 30m timeout if a pod
cannot become ready on any node. Add disableWait to install and
upgrade, matching the other DaemonSet-bearing charts (ceilometer,
libvirt, neutron, nova, openvswitch, pci-irq-affinity-agent).

Test Plan:
[PASS] Build stx-openstack-helm-fluxcd package
[PASS] Build application tarball
[PASS] Confirm osapi_volume_workers is 2 in the shipped
       cinder-static-overrides.yaml
[PASS] Apply on a standard system, 2 controllers and 3 computes:
       application reaches applied, 23 of 23 HelmReleases ready
[PASS] Confirm cinder-api renders processes = 2 in
       /etc/cinder/cinder-api-uwsgi.ini on a running pod
[PASS] Confirm every DaemonSet-bearing chart now sets disableWait on
       install and upgrade

Closes-Bug: 2162093
Change-Id: Ice144cf5d0b87c76e95c62450dc1457b17f9b45a
Signed-off-by: asyed1 <ahmed.syed@windriver.com>

revisions.message:
Refactor snapshot functions to use baomon commands

Replace shell logic in snapshot functions with direct baomon command
invocations. This eliminates duplicated logic and aligns with the
generation-based immutable secret storage model.

Changes:
- snapshotPreCheck: Use baomon snapshot precheck with kubectl pod discovery
  (getOpenbaoPods) instead of globalConfig.ServerAddresses for accurate data
- snapshotCreate: Already delegating to baomon; keep as-is
- snapshotSetSecret: Remove (logic now handled by baomon internally)
- snapshotRestore: Simplify to delegate to baomon snapshot restore;
  remove legacy cluster-key-* secret manipulation

Remove legacy helper functions (verified unused after snapshot functions removed):
- reconstructInitResponse: Only called by validateSecrets and snapshotSetSecret
- validateSecrets: Only called by snapshotSetSecret and snapshotRestore
- storeOpenbaoInitSecrets: Only called by snapshotRestore
- deleteShardSecrets: Only called by snapshotRestore
- splitShard: Only called by storeOpenbaoInitSecrets
- mergeKeyJson: Only called by reconstructInitResponse

Rationale:
These functions relied on legacy cluster-key-* mutable secret pattern where
unseal keys were split across 5 separate k8s secrets. With generation-based
immutable secrets (openbao-unseal-gen-001), baomon handles all operations
internally: metadata creation, validation, restoration, and tamper detection
via SHA-256 hashing.

The generation model eliminates the complexity of:
- Reconstructing init responses from split secrets
- Managing mutable secrets that could be partially updated
- Manual hash validation and cleanup

Test Plan:
- PASS    snapshotPreCheck validates all servers unsealed via baomon
- PASS    snapshotCreate delegates to baomon snapshot create command
- PASS    snapshotRestore delegates to baomon snapshot restore command
- PASS    Generation metadata stored as immutable k8s secrets
- PASS    Tamper detection via SHA-256 hash validation works correctly
- PASS    No cluster-key-* secret references remain in code

Add NVMe driver devstack plugin support

Introduce PCI_SIM_DEVICES so a stack can describe PF ownership and
personality explicitly instead of relying on the legacy even/odd PF
split.

The devstack wiring now falls into four pieces:
- topology parsing: parse service:personality entries, derive PF count,
  and re-parse on demand because DevStack re-sources lib/pci_sim across
  phases
- host bring-up: pass NVMe module args only when an NVMe PF is present
  and pre-arm cyborg:nvme VFs with driver_override so the host nvme
  driver stays active until VFIO handoff
- service wiring: reuse topology-aware VF selection for Nova
  alias/device_spec generation and for Cyborg PCI whitelist and NVMe
  driver config
- test fixtures: build UART and NVMe device profiles from the correct
  VF subset so mixed Cyborg topologies create matching resources

Auto-wire nvme_driver when PCI_SIM_DEVICES includes cyborg:nvme, keep
pci_driver limited to cyborg:uart, and propagate the same topology to
Tempest and the local.conf/devstack documentation updates.

revisions.message:
versioning: don't rewrite OPTIONS?version-id to the versions container

A CORS preflight for a versioned object was refused with a 401 even
when the origin was allowed on the container:

    OPTIONS /v1/a/c/o                  -> 200, Access-Control-Allow-Origin
    OPTIONS /v1/a/c/o?version-id=<id>  -> 401, no CORS headers

A ?version-id request has its path rewritten to the hidden versions
container. The proxy answers OPTIONS from the metadata of the container
in the request path, and the versions container is created without the
user's CORS config, so no origin is allowed.

An OPTIONS request is either a preflight or a query for the allowed
methods; neither answer depends on which version of the object is
wanted. Pass it through on the original path instead. The version-id is
still validated, so a malformed one is still a 400.

Closes-Bug: #2162973
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Change-Id: I69a425401bd5e36dfb1b18f3898e2e52aeb645f4
Signed-off-by: Christian Schwede <cschwede@mailbox.org>

revisions.message:
Support configurable docker filesystem sizes during bootstrap

Allow docker and docker-distribution filesystem sizes to be specified
via bootstrap overrides (docker_fs_size and
docker_distribution_fs_size). During bootstrap, puppet first applies the
configured sizes to the LVs via the manifest. After puppet completes,
the agent and conductor services start and read the actual LV sizes to
populate the database with the correct values rather than hardcoded
defaults.

ansible-playbooks:
- Add docker_fs_size and docker_distribution_fs_size as configurable
  bootstrap host_vars with documented defaults.
- Use the override values in the bootstrap manifest task.

config (sysinv):
- Read actual LV sizes for docker and docker-distribution filesystems at
  startup, falling back to defaults if the LVs are not yet created.
- Fix get_current_fs_size() to correctly resolve filesystem names to LV
  names using FILESYSTEM_LV_DICT, so callers can pass standard
filesystem name constants.

Test Plan:
- PASS: Added `docker_fs_size` and `docker_distribution_fs_size` to the
  bootstrap YAML to override the default values. After bootstrap, the
file system sizes were configured accordingly, and the SysInv database
was populated with the correct values from the parameters.
- PASS: The Docker file system uses the default size, and SysInv is
  populated with the default value when no `docker_fs_size` or
`docker_distribution_fs_size` overrides are provided.

Related review: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/config/+/1000015

ptp-notification: prefer leapfile from PTP config directory

Update LEAP_FILE_PATH resolution to check the PTP config directory
(/ptp/linuxptp/ptpinstance/leap-seconds.list) before falling back
to the zoneinfo mount (/usr/share/zoneinfo/leap-seconds.list).

On ostree-based systems, puppet copies the leapfile to
/etc/linuxptp/ptpinstance/ instead of /usr/share/zoneinfo/ (which
is read-only). The ptp-notification container already mounts host
/etc/ at /ptp/, so the file is accessible at the new path without
additional Helm chart changes.

The fallback to /usr/share/zoneinfo/ is retained for environments
that have not yet applied the puppet fix.

revisions.message:
sysinv: reconcile etcd cluster membership from an audit

The etcd cluster lifecycle operations added previously had no caller, so
the fixed members were never added during a deploy, never removed during
a rollback, and a simplex-to-duplex conversion never grew the cluster to
include the floating member.

Wire them up from a periodic audit rather than from a single event hook.
Each operation has to wait for the cluster to be reachable before it can
succeed, and that moment does not coincide with any one event: after a
conversion the floating instance can only be added once the seed is
serving, and during a deploy the fixed instances can only join once both
controllers run the new release. Driving this from an audit also means a
conversion or deploy that is interrupted is retried instead of leaving
the cluster short a member.

The audit dispatches on the deploy state and does nothing on any state it
does not recognise, so it stays clear of a deploy that is still moving:

  activate, activate-done                  add the fixed members
  activate-rollback, activate-rollback-done remove the fixed members
  no deploy in progress                    finish a simplex-to-duplex
                                           conversion, marker-guarded

Membership is left alone until the initial configuration is complete, and
while a backup or restore is running, because both relocate the etcd data
directories underneath the running cluster. The rollback path first checks
whether a fixed member is still registered, so a completed rollback does
not repeat the removal on every pass. Failures are logged and retried on
the next pass instead of propagating, and the existing cluster health
audit raises 850.003 if the cluster stays degraded.

Simplex runs a single fixed member and is skipped.

Test plan:
  PASS  flake8 clean at the enforced 120 column limit
  PASS  dispatch routes correctly for every deploy state, including the
        failed and pending states that must be left alone
  PASS  AIO-DX: floating member added after a simplex-to-duplex
        conversion, marker written, second pass is a no-op
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members added on deploy activate
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members removed on deploy activate-rollback
  PASS  audit is a no-op while a backup or restore is in progress

Story: 2010302
Task: 51206
Change-Id: I15988a73695f7d2846d67a4118a1f6fc75c6930b

_reconcile_etcd_rollback() matches members on peer URL as well as name.

etcd assigns a name only when a member starts and introduces itself, so a
member that was registered but never started lists with an empty name and its
peer URL alone identifying it. Matching on name alone made the remaining list
come back empty, _reconcile_etcd_rollback() returned without doing anything,
and activate-rollback completed having removed nothing -- leaving a stale
member registered against the cluster. Observed on duplex lab unr2603dx during
a 26.03.100 to 26.10 upgrade on build 631.

it, through cutils.format_url_address() so IPv6 addresses are bracketed.

changes that own those functions: remove_member() now accepts a peer URL and
looks the member up through find_member(), and
remove_fixed_etcd_members_for_rollback() passes it. Without those, detecting
the nameless member would have been followed by a removal that could not act
on it.

Test Plan:
  PASS  a member present only by peer URL is detected and the removal is
        invoked; both controller peer URLs are offered to the lookup.
  PASS  once no member remains the audit does not remove again, so repeated
        passes after a completed rollback are no-ops.
  PASS  IPv6 addresses are bracketed in the peer URL.
  PASS  pycodestyle count on test_manager.py unchanged at 345 and on

Change-Id: I15988a73695f7d2846d67a4118a1f6fc75c6930b
Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

sysinv: reconcile etcd cluster membership from an audit

The etcd cluster lifecycle operations added previously had no caller, so
the fixed members were never added during a deploy, never removed during
a rollback, and a simplex-to-duplex conversion never grew the cluster to
include the floating member.

Wire them up from a periodic audit rather than from a single event hook.
Each operation has to wait for the cluster to be reachable before it can
succeed, and that moment does not coincide with any one event: after a
conversion the floating instance can only be added once the seed is
serving, and during a deploy the fixed instances can only join once both
controllers run the new release. Driving this from an audit also means a
conversion or deploy that is interrupted is retried instead of leaving
the cluster short a member.

The design describes the conversion as triggered by the migration runtime
manifest when the system mode is set. That trigger on its own is not
sufficient here, because the manifest applies before the cluster is
necessarily reachable and an interrupted conversion would leave the
cluster short a member with nothing to retry it. The audit is idempotent
and acts only on recognised deploy states, so it complements that trigger
rather than replacing it.

The audit dispatches on the deploy state and does nothing on any state it
does not recognise, so it stays clear of a deploy that is still moving:

  activate, activate-done                  add the fixed members
  activate-rollback, activate-rollback-done remove the fixed members
  no deploy in progress                    finish a simplex-to-duplex
                                           conversion, marker-guarded

Membership is left alone until the initial configuration is complete, and
while a backup or restore is running, because both relocate the etcd data
directories underneath the running cluster. The rollback path first checks
whether a fixed member is still registered, so a completed rollback does
not repeat the removal on every pass. Failures are logged and retried on
the next pass instead of propagating.

Suppress the cluster health alarm while the topology is deliberately
changing. The health audit reports against the configured member count,
so through a deploy activate, a rollback or a conversion the registered
membership is by design below the configured membership and the alarm
would assert for the duration. That alarm gates locking the next
controller, so leaving it to fire would block the very procedure that is
driving the change. Those windows are governed by the sequencing and the
explicit health checks inside the procedures themselves. The same
suppression covers a backup or restore, and the period before the initial
configuration completes.

Simplex runs a single fixed member and is skipped.

Test plan:
  PASS  flake8 clean at the enforced 120 column limit
  PASS  dispatch routes correctly for every deploy state, including the
        failed and pending states that must be left alone
  PASS  health alarm suppressed on activate, activate-done,
        activate-rollback and activate-rollback-done, and not suppressed
        when no deploy is in progress or on an unrelated state
  PASS  health alarm suppressed while a backup or restore is running and
        before the initial configuration completes
  PASS  AIO-DX: floating member added after a simplex-to-duplex
        conversion, marker written, second pass is a no-op
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members added on deploy activate
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members removed on deploy activate-rollback
  PASS  audit is a no-op while a backup or restore is in progress

The audit also promotes a learner that has caught up, independently of the

Temporarily override the BMO checkout to dtantsur's cleaning-on-enroll
branch which adds a test that exercises automated cleaning on
enrollment.  This verifies that the autodetect deploy interface
correctly switches before cleaning.

This patch should NOT be merged - remove it from the chain once the
BMO test (metal3-io/baremetal-operator#3495) is merged into main.

revisions.message:
Fix inspect-tool crash on the map

Clicking a point with the map's inspect/selector tool threw

  The layer 'geojson-layer-<uuid>' does not exist in the map's
  style and cannot be queried for features

and no track list ever opened.

queryRenderedFeatures(bbox, {layers}) in MapLibre 5 throws on the
first id that is not in the style. react-map-gl, which the React
SPA passed interactiveLayerIds to, silently ignored unknown ids —
so the port inherited a list that was never required to be true.

It is not true. buildInteractiveLayerIds derived the clickable ids
from the wanted filter state, emitting geojson-layer-<grouping> for
every visible grouping, while syncTracks only adds those layers
when the filtered collection has features at all. A user whose
tracks are all served from pmtiles therefore has no geojson-tracks
source and no geojson-layer-* on the map, yet every one of them was
being queried. The same list also went stale between setStyle() and
'style.load', where the basemap switch has wiped the style but the
rebuild has not run yet.

Drop that second, divergent source of truth. managedTrackLayerIds
already records exactly what syncTracks put on the map, so the
click handler queries that, filtered through map.getLayer() as a
guard for the style-wiped window, via a new pure queryableLayerIds
helper. An empty result now skips the query instead of falling back
to querying every layer on the map — with no track layers present
there is nothing to inspect, and the fallback could match an
unrelated overlay source.

Both id paths the inspect flow depends on are preserved: geojson
features from geojson-tracks and vector-tile features from tile-*
and group-tile-* still resolve to track ids and reach onInspect.
The dive layers query nothing (they use DOM markers), so they had
no equivalent exposure.

Unit tests cover the helper over (wanted ids, present ids),
including the all-tiled and style-wiped cases.

revisions.message:
Add NVMe/FC support to the LVM/nvmet target

Teach the reference nvmet target helper to export volumes over NVMe over
Fibre Channel, selected with target_protocol=nvmet_fc. Unlike the RoCE
and TCP transports there is no target IP: the admin lists the FC target
port addresses in the new target_nvme_fc_traddrs option
(nn-0x<wwnn>:pn-0x<wwpn>), each of which must map to a local FC
target-mode port from an lpfc HBA in target mode or the in-kernel
nvme_fcloop loopback driver. The latter lets an NVMe-FC path run without
FC hardware, e.g. in CI.

The nvmet port is created with adrfam/trtype 'fc' and no trsvcid, and the
connection info carries fc portals as (traddr, 0, 'fc'). This requires
nvmeof_conn_info_version=2, which is enforced. No fabric zoning is
performed (use nvme_fcloop or a pre-zoned fabric), so no
initiator_target_map is emitted.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/os-brick/+/997815
Partial-Implements: blueprint nvme-fc-transport-support
Change-Id: I1c6a57196ba2f3159d543eb6d16632ec3b998323
Signed-off-by: Simon Dodsley <simon@purestorage.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add NVMe/FC (nvmet_fc) LVM CI job using nvme_fcloop

Add a cinder-tempest-plugin job,
cinder-tempest-plugin-lvm-nvmet-fc-barbican, that configures the LVM/nvmet
target over NVMe over Fibre Channel (target_protocol=nvmet_fc) and runs the
existing NVMe-oF tempest tests.  It mirrors the nvmet_tcp job but uses the
in-kernel nvme_fcloop loopback driver, set up in a new pre-run playbook
(playbooks/setup-nvme-fcloop.yaml), so a target+initiator FC pair exists on
a single node without any FC hardware.

The job runs in the check pipeline as non-voting during rollout: it needs
the os-brick NVMe/FC transport support and the LVM/nvmet NVMe/FC driver
support to be present, and the exact fcloop sysfs setup is kernel-version
dependent.

Move TLS parameter setup from activate to migrate phase

The 42-add-tls-parameters upgrade script previously ran during
deploy-activate using the sysinv API. It called
service_parameter.apply('kubernetes') which triggered a puppet
manifest and kube-apiserver restart, then polled for ~2m45s
waiting for the apiserver to come back with a new PID.

Moved the script to the migrate phase (deploy-start) using direct
PostgreSQL inserts/updates. Platform TLS params are applied by
puppet on host unlock via the normal config-target mechanism.
Kubernetes kube_apiserver params are applied by a
companion change in stx-puppet that conditionally includes
change_apiserver_parameters during USM upgrade unlock.

This eliminates the ~2m45s kube-apiserver restart polling from
deploy-activate entirely.

revisions.message:
Delegate STX-O backup and restore to application

The STX-O backup and restore logic lives in the platform ansible
repository. Application-level changes require a platform change to
follow, which has produced defects where the platform playbooks drifted
from the application (e.g. Bug 2152622, Bug 2153526).

Add a delegation check to restore_openstack.yml and to the OpenStack
section of the backup-system role. When the application ships its own
playbooks at /opt/platform/ansible/<release>/<app-name>/current/
backup-restore/, delegate to them via include_tasks. Otherwise the
existing inline logic runs unchanged as a fallback.

include_tasks is used instead of import_tasks because import_tasks
resolves the file path at parse time, before the when condition is
evaluated. With no application playbook deployed, parse-time resolution
would fail and the fallback would never be reachable.

Restore side: the delegation check needs software_version, which is
produced by backup-restore/prepare-env. That role was previously only
reached through restore-openstack/prepare-env, which runs too late and
is skipped on the continuation pass. Import common/prepare-env and
backup-restore/prepare-env as pre_tasks so host connectivity and
platform context are available before the check. Both are idempotent.

Backup side: the staging directories (mariadb_dir, helm_overrides)
are created by the platform playbook before the delegation check so
the paths are known whichever side writes the dumps. Detecting whether
the application is present also stays with the platform, since it gates
the archive size estimation, tarball creation and transfer.

Also remove helm_overrides_sqldump_dir from the platform tarball target
list (final_backup_targets). That entry was dead code: the STX-O
restore extracts all artifacts from the STX-O tarball exclusively, the
companion mariadb_dir was never in the platform targets, and the
helm_overrides table is already captured by the sysinv pg_dump which
the platform restore replays in full.

Backward compatible: an application that does not ship playbooks keeps
using the inline logic. Forward compatible: an older platform release
ignores the deployed playbooks.

       and backup.yml

       and backup-restore/prepare-env run before the delegation check

[PASS] Delegation and fallback branches validated in local sandbox

Add NVMe/FC (nvmet_fc) LVM CI job using nvme_fcloop

Add a cinder-tempest-plugin job,
cinder-tempest-plugin-lvm-nvmet-fc-barbican, that configures the LVM/nvmet
target over NVMe over Fibre Channel (target_protocol=nvmet_fc) and runs the
existing NVMe-oF tempest tests.  It mirrors the nvmet_tcp job but uses the
in-kernel nvme_fcloop loopback driver, set up in a new pre-run playbook
(playbooks/setup-nvme-fcloop.yaml), so a target+initiator FC pair exists on
a single node without any FC hardware.

The job runs in the check pipeline as non-voting during rollout: it needs
the os-brick NVMe/FC transport support and the LVM/nvmet NVMe/FC driver
support to be present, and the exact fcloop sysfs setup is kernel-version
dependent.

revisions.message:
etcd: convert a simplex system to duplex

The conversion renames the incumbent member to fixed-0, keeping its
data, and registers the floating member against it -- the order a fresh
duplex bootstrap uses, rather than the reverse.

The address pools are updated around the mode change, not after it:
management, OAM and admin are writable while the host is locked and are
set first, because the runtime manifests that "system modify -m duplex"
fires read them. sysinv holds cluster-host, pxeboot and storage
read-only until the mode is already duplex and the migration capability
is set, so those are updated afterwards, still ahead of the unlock.

The unlock reboots into a system whose DRBD resource files, haproxy
config and etcd membership all name controller-0's unit addresses,
while /etc/network/interfaces.d carries only the floating ones. DRBD
then cannot start. They are therefore placed and written to disk before
the reboot.

The sm-api-internal frontend is moved off the floating address so
haproxy can bind while the platform services still hold it, and the USM
endpoint is waited for explicitly -- without it the unlock is rejected
with CannotQueryPlatformUpgrade and the reason is not obvious.

revisions.message:
etcd: convert a simplex system to duplex

The conversion renames the incumbent member to fixed-0, keeping the
data it already holds, and registers the floating member against it.
That is the order a fresh duplex bootstrap uses: the member with the
data seeds the cluster and the new one joins, rather than the reverse.

etcd has no rename -- identity lives in the raft state, not the
directory name -- so the rename goes through a snapshot restore with
--name.

The renamed member keeps an address that exists. The cluster-host pool
is still empty while the conversion runs, because sysinv opens it only
once the mode is duplex and the simplex_to_duplex_migration capability
is set, and the mode change is what fires this manifest. Loopback
carries the member until the unlock moves it to controller-0's unit
address, which is the transition a fresh duplex already performs.

Change-Id: Ie2c570c48e7de62e2b72fc6a5bfd3bd5194ef94a
Signed-off-by: aahuja <Abhishek.Ahuja@windriver.com>

etcd: convert a simplex system to duplex

The conversion renames the incumbent member to fixed-0, keeping the
data it already holds, and registers the floating member against it.
That is the order a fresh duplex bootstrap uses: the member with the
data seeds the cluster and the new one joins, rather than the reverse.

etcd has no rename -- identity lives in the raft state, not the
directory name -- so the rename goes through a snapshot restore with
--name.

The renamed member keeps an address that exists. The cluster-host pool
is still empty while the conversion runs, because sysinv opens it only
once the mode is duplex and the simplex_to_duplex_migration capability
is set, and the mode change is what fires this manifest. Loopback
carries the member until the unlock moves it to controller-0's unit
address, which is the transition a fresh duplex already performs.

drbd: create cephmon metadata on first-time setup. Adding the ceph
backend while every controller is still locked leaves the drbd-cephmon
resource with no metadata. Create the metadata when this node has not
been ceph-configured before, without taking the resource Primary.

revisions.message:
Shade visited regions on the editor map

The editor's boundary treatment took the lines only: mergeBoundaryStyle
with includeVisited false, because nothing editor-side ever fetched
anyone's visited regions, so those layers could only have cost six
sources' worth of tile requests for pixels they would never draw.

That is now the single visual difference between the two map surfaces,
and step 3 of doc/plans/editor-map-convergence.md is where it goes
away. e2e/map-filters.spec.ts pins it from the other side: it waits for
visited-countries-fill to come back after a basemap switch, which is
the machine-checkable form of "the engines have converged".

The decision splits along its natural seam. Which layers a style
carries is a build-time question, so it stays in the style — a basemap
switch rebuilds the style and the visited layers come back with it, no
imperative re-add to get wrong. Which regions they match is a data
question, so it is a setFilter per layer; baking the filters in too
would turn every visited-regions update into a full style rebuild,
tearing down every imperative layer on the map to change two
expressions.

Off for an anonymous session, hard: api.ts bounces the page on a 401,
and throwing a signed-out visitor out of the editor mid-edit is the
trap "My Tracks" already documents. Signed in, the layers go on however
empty the data is, exactly as /map has always drawn them — presence
that depends on the data would make the layer set jump around as trips
are added. The fetch shares /map's resource key, so the panel that
arrives next costs no second request and its group-scoped refetches
reshade the map for free.

Labels follow the basemap's own, and a style with no font endpoint gets
none at all: MapLibre reports a symbol layer without glyphs per tile
rather than quietly not drawing it.

wiring that supplies the real map, fetch and flag, and is deliberately

same canvas. Asserting that on /map would have stayed green with this
entire integration removed.

none at all: MapLibre reports a symbol layer without glyphs per tile
rather than quietly not drawing it.

The live half is a store-free state machine over injected dependencies
(map/visited-boundary-sync.ts), so studio/tests drives the whole
sequence a session goes through — sign in, data arrives, the one style
rebuild that flip is worth, filters landing on style.load, a group
toggle updating them in place with no second rebuild, sign out
dropping the subscription and the layers. editor-boundaries.ts is the
wiring that supplies the real map, fetch and flag, and is deliberately
nothing else.

e2e covers it on the surface this changes rather than on the one that
already had it: e2e/editor-map.spec.ts loads /app signed in, waits for
visited-countries-fill, switches basemap and waits for it again on the
same canvas. Asserting that on /map would have stayed green with this
entire integration removed.

dpll-mgr: add sd_notify lifecycle, watchdog, and config validation

Add sd_notify("READY=1") after successful initialization (config
parsed and validated, DPLL netlink connected). This enables
Type=notify in the systemd unit for accurate startup detection.

Add sd_notify("WATCHDOG=1") at the end of each main loop iteration
(event-based and poll-based) to support WatchdogSec hang detection.
If the main loop hangs (e.g. dead netlink socket with no error
return), systemd will automatically restart the service after the
configured 30s timeout.

Add sd_notify("STOPPING=1") on graceful shutdown to inform systemd
the service is intentionally exiting.

Add config_validate() for field-level semantic validation after
JSON parsing. Required fields (dpll0 device, pin_priority_map,
ptp_bh UDS channel, holdover tiers, ptp_primary_attributes) are
checked with specific error messages naming the missing field.
All errors are reported before exit (not just the first).

Link against libsystemd and add libsystemd-dev to Build-Depends.

dpll-mgr: add sd_notify lifecycle, watchdog, and config validation

Add sd_notify("READY=1") after DPLL netlink initialization and
device discovery completes. This fires before the PTP-GM connection
check, which may take several seconds or fail entirely when no GM
is available. The daemon is considered ready once the DPLL subsystem
is operational. This enables Type=notify in the systemd unit for
accurate startup detection.

Make the PTP-GM connection check non-fatal: if no grandmaster is
connected at startup, log a warning and proceed to the main loop
where the UDS reconnect/backoff mechanism will retry. Previously
the daemon exited immediately, preventing service stability on
systems where ptp4l takes time to acquire a GM.

Add sd_notify("WATCHDOG=1") at the end of each main loop iteration
(event-based and poll-based) to support WatchdogSec hang detection.
If the main loop hangs, systemd will restart the service after the
configured timeout.

Add sd_notify("STOPPING=1") on graceful shutdown to inform systemd
the service is intentionally exiting.

Add config_validate() for field-level semantic validation after
JSON parsing. Required fields (dpll0 device, pin_priority_map,
ptp_bh UDS channel, holdover tiers, ptp_primary_attributes) are
checked with specific error messages naming the missing field.
All errors are reported before exit (not just the first).

Fix YNL netlink attribute length encoding for kernel 6.18
compatibility. Use exact byte count (NLA_HDRLEN + len + 1) rather
than NLA_ALIGN-padded length, which triggers EINVAL from stricter
policy validation in newer kernels.

Link against libsystemd and add libsystemd-dev to Build-Depends.

revisions.message:
Add source_ports param for synce4l ext_src relay

Add source_ports to the synce4l_params whitelist so it is passed
through to the ext_src section in the rendered config file. This
parameter enables QL pass-through from specified ports in DPLL
netlink mode on E825/GNR-D platforms, where the recovered clock
input is represented as an external source.

When source_ports is configured on an ext_src, synce4l reads the
live RX QL from the listed ports instead of using the static
input_QL value, enabling ESMC relay behavior.

Also fix a bug where _set_external_source_parameters() is called
once per interface in the instance loop. When a ptp-interface has
multiple underlying interfaces (e.g. pxeboot0 + eno8303), the
external_source meta parameter is consumed on the first iteration
and the second iteration returns an empty dict that overwrites the
valid result. Fix by only updating external_source when the
function returns a non-empty result.

Test Plan:

      rendered synce4l config under the ext_src section
PASS: synce4l reads source_ports and relays upstream QL to TX
PASS: ptp-instance-apply generates [{ext_src}] section correctly
      on multi-interface ptp-interface (pxeboot0 + eno8303)

Network: Add ip_availability_details field

The Neutron ``network-ip-availability-details`` extension[0] adds an
``ip_availability_details`` attribute to the network-ip-availabilities
resource. It reports the total and used IP counts separately for the
subnet CIDRs and for the subnet allocation pools, which the existing
``total_ips`` and ``used_ips`` fields cannot express on their own:
``total_ips`` is relative to the allocation pools when a subnet has any,
while ``used_ips`` is always relative to the whole subnet.

Add the attribute to the ``NetworkIPAvailability`` resource.

Add Audit Pipeline client support (microversion 1.8)

Implement python-watcherclient support for the new Audit Pipeline
resource introduced in Watcher API microversion 1.8.

New v1 client and OSC commands:

* auditpipeline create  -- create and trigger a ONESHOT CASCADE pipeline;
stages are passed as a JSON list referencing Audit Templates by UUID
or name (``audit_template`` field)
* auditpipeline list    -- list pipelines with optional --detail flag
* auditpipeline show    -- show pipeline with formatted stage details
* auditpipeline update  -- update name / auto_trigger (PENDING only)
* auditpipeline cancel  -- cancel a PENDING or ONGOING pipeline (202)
* auditpipeline delete  -- delete from SUCCEEDED, FAILED, or CANCELLED

Stage details (position, goal name, strategy name) are rendered via
StagesColumn — human-readable in table/shell output, raw list in
JSON/YAML output.

Other changes:

* api_versioning: add MINOR_8_AUDIT_PIPELINE constant and
allow_audit_pipeline() version check helper
* Bump API_MAX_VERSION to 1.8
* setup.cfg: register all six auditpipeline entry points under both
openstack.cli.extension and infra_optim.v1
* doc/source/cli/details.rst: document all six commands
* unit tests: TestStagesColumn and AuditPipelineShellTest covering

revisions.message:
Scale DaemonSet rollouts and restore accurate apply status

Every DaemonSet-bearing chart in the application pins
max_unavailable: 1, so a rolling update replaces pods one node at a
time and rollout duration grows linearly with the number of
openstack-labelled compute nodes. On a 102-node system this puts
several charts far beyond the 30m timeout set on each HelmRelease:
openvswitch takes roughly 3.5 hours and libvirt roughly 2.5 at
measured per-pod cycle times, and nova-compute needs about 44 minutes
on its largest host group. Raising the timeout only relocates the
wall, because the duration stays proportional to node count.

That timeout failure was previously avoided by setting
disableWait: true on the affected releases, which introduced a second
and worse problem. Flux reports such a release Ready as soon as the
manifests are accepted, before any pod has been replaced. Because
sysinv treats the HelmRelease Ready condition as its source of truth,
the application is reported applied and the apply-in-progress alarm is
cleared while pods are still cycling. The documented verification step
of checking that HelmReleases report READY=True passes in that state,
so it does not detect an incomplete rollout. The semantic checks that
reject host-unlock and host-swact during an apply are released at the
same moment, so those operations are accepted while replacements are
still in flight. A pod that fails to start or crash-loops during the
rollout is not surfaced as a release failure, because nothing is
waiting on readiness.

Fix both together, since the second cannot be fixed without the
first.

Express max_unavailable as 10% on libvirt, openvswitch, ceilometer,
nova and pci-irq-affinity-agent. Kubernetes resolves a DaemonSet
maxUnavailable percentage by rounding up against
status.desiredNumberScheduled, so the wave count becomes ceil(1/p)
and is independent of node count: any of these charts completes in
about ten waves whether the system has twenty compute nodes or two
hundred. Duration therefore stops being a function of scale and
becomes a function of per-pod cycle time alone.

Template updateStrategy and minReadySeconds in the
pci-irq-affinity-agent chart. It emitted no updateStrategy at all, so
the rendered object fell back to the Kubernetes default of
maxUnavailable: 1 and no override could reach it. The failure mode was
silent: an override was accepted and displayed by helm-override-show
while the rendered DaemonSet stayed unchanged. The chart defaults are
left at max_unavailable: 1, so the template change alone is
behaviour-neutral and only makes the value reachable; the value itself
comes from the static overrides.

Set disableWait to false on libvirt, openvswitch,
pci-irq-affinity-agent and nova. With the rollouts now fitting the
existing 30m timeout, the wait no longer causes the failure it was
introduced to avoid. The deployed helm-controller uses the kstatus
poller wait strategy, which already treats a DaemonSet as current only
when the observed generation matches and updatedNumberScheduled equals
desiredNumberScheduled, so no custom health-check expressions are
needed to make the wait correct.

Because a percentage rounds up with a floor of one, systems with one
or two compute nodes resolve to 1 and behave exactly as before, so no
special case is needed for AIO configurations. Absolute concurrency
does grow with node count, which is deliberate: 10% is two nodes at
twenty and twenty nodes at two hundred.

The neutron agents are left at max_unavailable: 1. Their largest host
group completes in about 16 minutes at that setting, so they were
never at risk, and raising them would not reduce the interaction
described below. The ceilometer release keeps disableWait: true: its
compute DaemonSet does not exist on the currently supported update
source, so on that path it is a fresh install rather than a rolling
update, maxUnavailable does not govern DaemonSet creation, and waiting
on 102 simultaneous pod creations has not been characterised. The
eight non-DaemonSet releases that also carry disableWait: true are
untouched; they predate this defect and their reasons are not
recorded, so each needs its own assessment.

Readiness and liveness probe settings are unchanged, min_ready_seconds
stays at 0, no HelmRelease timeout or interval value changes, and no
dependsOn ordering is added. The Deployment rolling-update path is
untouched; its replica counts track controllers rather than compute
nodes and it has no equivalent exposure.

One behavioural consequence should be recorded. Restarting an
openvswitch pod interrupts instance network connectivity on that node
for roughly three seconds, because the OVS kernel datapath keeps
forwarding on cached flows while ovs-vswitchd restarts. That cost is
per-node and is already paid on every application update today; this
change does not increase it, but it does compress those interruptions
from hours into minutes. Separately, when a node's openvswitch and
neutron-ovs-agent pods are replaced within about sixteen seconds of
each other, the datapath loses userspace flow state while the agent
that would reprogram it is unavailable, and connectivity is
interrupted for 25 to 30 seconds instead. Measured on roughly 11% of
nodes at these values. Ordering the openvswitch and neutron releases
would remove that coincidence and is proposed separately.

Test Plan:

Standard configuration, 2 controllers, 102 openstack-labelled compute
nodes, 500 running instances. Rollout duration and concurrency:
  PASS - libvirt full rollout in 11m45s at 11 concurrent, against a
         predicted 12.3m
  PASS - openvswitch full rollout in 17m47s at 11 concurrent, against
         a predicted 20.8m
  PASS - pci-irq-affinity-agent full rollout in 18m32s at 11
         concurrent, against a predicted 21.2m
  PASS - nova-compute full rollout in 5m36s, 7 concurrent on its
         largest host group and 14 across all seven
  PASS - all four charts complete inside the 30m HelmRelease timeout
  PASS - per-pod cycle time does not degrade with concurrency;
         measured wave intervals were below the single-replacement
         baseline on every chart
  PASS - all 500 instances remain ACTIVE throughout every rollout

Percentage resolution, same configuration:
  PASS - a 102-pod DaemonSet resolves 10% to 11
  PASS - an 8-pod host group resolves 10% to 1, confirming round-up
         with a floor of one
  PASS - a 14-pod host group resolves 10% to 2
  PASS - percentage accepted as a string by the IntOrString field

pci-irq-affinity-agent chart rendering:
  PASS - renders maxUnavailable: 1 as an integer from the default
  PASS - renders maxUnavailable: 10% as a string from the override
  PASS - omits updateStrategy and minReadySeconds when the entry is
         disabled
  PASS - omits the rollingUpdate block when pod_replacement_strategy
         is not RollingUpdate
  PASS - rendered output byte-identical to the pre-change chart when
         defaults are used
  PASS - the static override reaches the rendered DaemonSet, which the
         chart could not do before

Instance impact, probed by TCP connect at sub-second resolution:
  PASS - libvirt, zero failed connections across 52481 samples during
         a full rollout
  PASS - pci-irq-affinity-agent, zero failed connections across 83221
         samples during a full rollout
  PASS - openvswitch, interruption of 2.2 to 3.8 seconds per node on
         bare-metal nodes, one occurrence per node, matching the
         single-replacement baseline
  FAIL* - openvswitch concurrent with neutron-ovs-agent, interruption
         of 25 to 30 seconds on nodes where both pods are replaced
         within about sixteen seconds

Status accuracy, same configuration:
  <TO BE COMPLETED FROM THE UPGRADE RUN — see the four items below>
  - each affected release reports READY=True only after its DaemonSet
    reports updatedNumberScheduled equal to desiredNumberScheduled
  - sysinv reports the application applying until every DaemonSet
    rollout has completed
  - the apply-in-progress alarm stays raised for the duration
  - host-unlock and host-swact continue to be rejected while rollouts
    are in flight

Failure handling:
  <TO BE COMPLETED — a pod forced into a crash loop must cause the
   owning release to report a failure and the apply to fail, and the
   existing recovery path must restore the previous version>

Regression:
  PASS - neutron agents unchanged at max_unavailable: 1 and unaffected
  PASS - Deployment rolling-update values unchanged
  PASS - ceilometer disableWait unchanged
  PASS - the eight non-DaemonSet releases carrying disableWait
         unchanged
  PASS - HelmRelease timeout and interval values unchanged
  PASS - unlabelled compute nodes excluded from all these DaemonSets
  PASS - instances on nodes outside the current wave keep
         uninterrupted connectivity
  SKIP** - AIO-SX and two-node configurations

* Not a regression introduced by these values. The interaction
  requires both pods to be replaced within a short window and is
  possible at the current setting too; compressing the openvswitch
  rollout makes the coincidence more likely, from roughly one node to
  roughly eleven at this scale. Adding a dependsOn between the
  openvswitch and neutron releases removes it, and is proposed
  separately so that this change can be evaluated on its own.

** Not exercised on a single-node or two-node system. The floor-of-one
   behaviour those configurations rely on is covered by the 8-pod host
   group result above, which resolves 10% to 1.

References:

[1] DaemonSet maxUnavailable percentages round up against
    status.desiredNumberScheduled
    https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/daemon-set-v1/
[2] Deployment maxUnavailable rounds down while maxSurge rounds up,
    the opposite convention, which is why the two paths cannot share a
    value
    https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/
[3] helm-controller HelmRelease v2 spec, install and upgrade
    disableWait and the wait strategy
    https://github.com/fluxcd/helm-controller/blob/main/docs/spec/v2/helmreleases.md

Signed-off-by: ssajeev <sravan.sajeev@windriver.com>

Scale DaemonSet rollouts and restore accurate apply status

Every DaemonSet-bearing chart in the application pins
max_unavailable: 1, so a rolling update replaces pods one node at a
time and rollout duration grows linearly with the number of
openstack-labelled compute nodes. On a 102-node system this puts
several charts far beyond the 30m timeout set on each HelmRelease:
openvswitch takes roughly 3.5 hours and libvirt roughly 2.5 at
measured per-pod cycle times. nova-compute needs about 44 minutes on
its largest host group; that release does not wait, so it is not a
timeout breach, but it is 44 minutes in which the application is
reported applied while pods are still cycling. Raising the timeout
only relocates the wall, because the duration stays proportional to
node count.

That timeout failure was previously avoided by setting
disableWait: true on the affected releases, which introduced a second
and worse problem. Flux reports such a release Ready as soon as the
manifests are accepted, before any pod has been replaced. Because
sysinv treats the HelmRelease Ready condition as its source of truth,
the application is reported applied and the apply-in-progress alarm is
cleared while pods are still cycling. The documented verification step
of checking that HelmReleases report READY=True passes in that state,
so it does not detect an incomplete rollout. The semantic checks that
reject host-unlock and host-swact during an apply are released at the
same moment, so those operations are accepted while replacements are
still in flight. A pod that fails to start or crash-loops during the
rollout is not surfaced as a release failure, because nothing is
waiting on readiness.

Fix both together, since the second cannot be fixed without the
first.

Express max_unavailable as 10% on libvirt, openvswitch, ceilometer,
nova and pci-irq-affinity-agent. Kubernetes resolves a DaemonSet
maxUnavailable percentage by rounding up against
status.desiredNumberScheduled, so the wave count becomes ceil(1/p)
and is independent of node count: any of these charts completes in
about ten waves whether the system has twenty compute nodes or two
hundred. Duration therefore stops being a function of scale and
becomes a function of per-pod cycle time alone.

Template updateStrategy and minReadySeconds in the
pci-irq-affinity-agent chart. It emitted no updateStrategy at all, so
the rendered object fell back to the Kubernetes default of
maxUnavailable: 1 and no override could reach it. The failure mode was
silent: an override was accepted and displayed by helm-override-show
while the rendered DaemonSet stayed unchanged. The chart defaults are
left at max_unavailable: 1, so the template change alone is
behaviour-neutral and only makes the value reachable; the value itself
comes from the static overrides.

Set disableWait to false on libvirt, openvswitch and
pci-irq-affinity-agent. With the rollouts now fitting the existing 30m
timeout, the wait no longer causes the failure it was introduced to
avoid. Both the kstatus poller strategy and Helm's built-in readiness
check treat a DaemonSet as ready only when the observed generation
matches and updatedNumberScheduled and numberReady equal
desiredNumberScheduled, so the wait is correct under either strategy
and no custom health-check expressions are needed.

Nova is deliberately excluded and keeps disableWait: true.
nova-db-sync and nova-rabbit-init are declared as post-install and
post-upgrade Helm hooks, and nova-compute's init container lists both
as kubernetes-entrypoint dependencies. Helm runs the readiness wait
before the post-upgrade hook phase, so with disableWait: false the
newly created nova-compute pods block on jobs that Helm has not
created yet, and the release deadlocks until the timeout. This is
scale-independent and would deadlock on a single-node system. Nova
therefore yields no status-accuracy improvement. It still moves to
10%, which shortens the window in which the application is
misreported as applied from about 44 minutes to under six. The
HelmRelease carries a comment recording the constraint.

The rule this establishes: a DaemonSet may take disableWait: false
only if no init-container dependency resolves to a resource created
in that same release's post-upgrade hook phase.

Add a dependsOn from the neutron release to openvswitch, so the two
DaemonSet rollouts are serialised rather than concurrent. Both charts
place a pod on every compute node and both previously depended only on
placement, so Flux reconciled them at the same time with nothing
coordinating which node each was working on. This removes the
interaction described below rather than reducing its probability. It
costs nothing against the timeout, because the timeout is per
HelmRelease and each release still fits its own window: openvswitch in
about 18 minutes and the largest neutron agent group in about 14.

That ordering only takes effect because openvswitch carries
disableWait: false. dependsOn gates on the dependency reporting Ready,
and a release with disableWait: true reports Ready immediately, so
restoring that flag on openvswitch would silently reduce the ordering
to a no-op. The reverse direction does not work for the same reason,
since neutron carries disableWait: true. Both files carry a comment
recording this coupling.

Because a percentage rounds up with a floor of one, systems with one
or two compute nodes resolve to 1 and behave exactly as before, so no
special case is needed for AIO configurations. Absolute concurrency
does grow with node count, which is deliberate: 10% is two nodes at
twenty and twenty nodes at two hundred.

The neutron agents are left at max_unavailable: 1. Their largest host
group completes in about 16 minutes at that setting, so they were
never at risk, and raising them would not reduce the interaction
described below. The ceilometer release keeps disableWait: true: its
compute DaemonSet does not exist on the currently supported update
source, so on that path it is a fresh install rather than a rolling
update, maxUnavailable does not govern DaemonSet creation, and waiting
on 102 simultaneous pod creations has not been characterised. The
remaining releases that carry disableWait: true are untouched. Their
reasons predate this defect and are not recorded, nova excepted, so
each of the others needs its own assessment.

Readiness and liveness probe settings are unchanged, min_ready_seconds
stays at 0, and no HelmRelease timeout or interval value changes. The
Deployment rolling-update path is untouched; its replica counts track
controllers rather than compute nodes and it has no equivalent
exposure. The new dependsOn also serialises these two releases on a
fresh install, not only on an update, which lengthens a fresh apply by
roughly the openvswitch install duration.

One behavioural consequence should be recorded. Restarting an
openvswitch pod interrupts instance network connectivity on that node
for roughly three seconds, because the OVS kernel datapath keeps
forwarding on cached flows while ovs-vswitchd restarts. That cost is
per-node and is already paid on every application update today; this
change does not increase it, but it does compress those interruptions
from hours into minutes, so more nodes are affected at the same moment.
Separately, when a node's openvswitch and neutron-ovs-agent pods are
replaced within about sixteen seconds of each other, the datapath
loses userspace flow state while the agent that would reprogram it is
unavailable, and connectivity is interrupted for 25 to 30 seconds
instead. That was measured on roughly 11% of nodes before the
dependsOn ordering was added, and is the reason the ordering is part
of this change.

Scale libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent rollouts, restore waits

Every DaemonSet-bearing chart in the application pins
max_unavailable: 1, so a rolling update replaces pods one node at a
time and rollout duration grows linearly with the number of
openstack-labelled compute nodes. Against the 30m timeout each
HelmRelease carries, several charts are far outside it at 102-node
scale: libvirt takes about 2h06m and openvswitch was measured at
3h07m on a serial rollback of that DaemonSet. Raising the timeout only
relocates the wall, because the duration stays proportional to node
count.

That timeout breach is currently avoided by setting disableWait: true
on the affected releases, which trades it for a worse problem. Flux
reports such a release Ready as soon as the manifests are accepted,
before any pod has been replaced. Because sysinv treats the
HelmRelease Ready condition as its source of truth, the application is
reported applied and the apply-in-progress alarm is cleared while pods
are still cycling. The documented verification step of checking that
HelmReleases report READY=True passes in that state, so it does not
detect an incomplete rollout. The semantic checks that reject
host-unlock and host-swact during an apply are released at the same
moment, so those operations are accepted while replacements are still
in flight. A pod that crash-loops during the rollout is not surfaced
as a release failure, because nothing is waiting on readiness.

The two properties are coupled: a release can only be made to wait
once its rollout fits the timeout. Fix them together, for the charts
where doing so carries no service impact.

Template updateStrategy and minReadySeconds in the
pci-irq-affinity-agent chart. It emitted no updateStrategy at all, so
the rendered object fell back to the Kubernetes default of
maxUnavailable: 1 and no override could reach it. The failure mode was
silent: an override was accepted and displayed by helm-override-show
while the rendered DaemonSet stayed unchanged. The chart default is
left at max_unavailable: 1, so the template change alone is
behaviour-neutral and only makes the value reachable.

Express max_unavailable as 10% on libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent,
and set disableWait to false on both. Kubernetes resolves a DaemonSet
maxUnavailable percentage by rounding up against
status.desiredNumberScheduled, so the wave count becomes ceil(1/p) and
is independent of node count: either chart completes in about ten waves
whether the system has twenty compute nodes or two hundred. libvirt
goes from 2h06m to 11m45s, which fits the existing timeout, so the wait
no longer causes the failure it was introduced to avoid. Both charts
are node-local -- neither carries the dataplane -- so parallelising
them has no effect on instance connectivity. Both the kstatus poller
strategy and Helm's built-in readiness check treat a DaemonSet as ready
only when the observed generation matches and updatedNumberScheduled
and numberReady equal desiredNumberScheduled, so the wait is correct
under either strategy and no custom health-check expressions are
needed.

Express max_unavailable as 10% on ceilometer, which keeps
disableWait: true. This value is inert on the currently supported
update source, where the ceilometer compute DaemonSet does not exist
and is therefore created rather than rolled. It is set because the
value shipped in a release paces the update paths that follow it:
recovery applies the charts of the release being recovered *to*, so
this is what will govern both the next forward rollout and a rollback
into this release. At 1 that is roughly three hours of the application
being reported applied while pods are still cycling; at 10% it is
under twenty minutes. Neither can breach the release timeout, because
nothing waits on the rollout.

Add a dependsOn from the nova release to libvirt. nova-compute's init
container lists a same-host libvirt pod under
dependencies.static.compute.pod with requireSameNode: true, so a nova
pod cannot start until the libvirt pod on its own node is ready.
Without this edge the two releases are unordered siblings under
placement and Flux reconciles them concurrently, so a nova pod can land
on a node whose libvirt pod is mid-replacement and stall until it
becomes ready. This makes the release graph express a dependency the
charts already have. It is safe in every supported configuration:
libvirt has no _is_enabled override and never removes its own
HelmRelease, so the target always exists wherever nova is deployed. The
edge also holds with nova on disableWait: true, because dependsOn gates
on the dependency reporting Ready, not on the depending release's own
flag, and libvirt now gates genuinely.

The rule this establishes, and the one the current state violates: a
chart either waits and is parallelised, or does not wait and stays
serial. Nothing should wait on a serial rollout at scale, and nothing
parallelised should go unwatched. libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent
move into the first category; every other DaemonSet-bearing chart is
left in the second, so this change does not carry the existing defect
forward on any chart it touches.

Non-effects.

The openvswitch release is unchanged and carries only a comment. It is
deferred for service impact, not for timeout. When a node has its
openvswitch and neutron-ovs-agent pods replaced within about sixteen
seconds of each other, the OVS kernel datapath loses its userspace flow
state while the agent that would reprogram it is also unavailable, and
instance connectivity on that node drops for 25 to 30 seconds instead
of the usual three. Exposure scales with how much of this rollout
overlaps neutron's: at three hours only a small part of the run
overlaps neutron's fifteen minutes and roughly one node is affected,
but compressed to about eighteen minutes nearly every node's
replacement falls inside neutron's window, and the figure measured at
102-node scale was about 11%. Ordering the two releases removes the
interaction rather than reducing its probability, so scaling this chart
is deferred to the change that lands that ordering.

The neutron release is unchanged and carries only a comment, for two
separate reasons. A dependsOn entry naming openvswitch cannot be
declared: when OVS runs with DPDK the dataplane is managed on the host
and the openvswitch chart is not deployed at all, because
OpenvswitchHelm._is_enabled returns False and execute_kustomize_updates
then calls helm_release_resource_delete to remove the HelmRelease from
the kustomization. Naming a HelmRelease that does not exist leaves the
depending release permanently unreconciled, so the application apply
would never complete on any DPDK deployment. The two conditions do not
overlap -- the connectivity interaction requires a containerised
openvswitch pod, which is exactly the configuration in which the
dependency would be valid -- so a conditional edge added under the same
predicate that governs the chart is correct rather than a compromise.
It needs a dependency-removal method alongside
helm_release_resource_delete in sysinv/helm/kustomize_base.py and an
execute_kustomize_updates hook in the neutron plugin, neither of which
exists yet.

The neutron agents also stay at max_unavailable: 1, and not because
they fit the timeout. The largest agent group on the measured system is
62 pods, about 16.5 minutes, but only because its 102 nodes split into
nested and bare-metal host groups; on a homogeneous 100-node system
that group is roughly 100 pods and about 35 minutes, which breaches.
The durable reason is scoping rather than duration: l3-agent and
dhcp-agent are router- and network-scoped, and with
max_l3_agents_per_router: 1 and l3_ha: false, eleven concurrent
replacements means eleven routers each losing their only agent. These
agents need per-agent values, not a single chart-wide one.

The nova release keeps max_unavailable: 1 and disableWait: true, and
carries a comment recording why. nova-db-sync and nova-rabbit-init are
declared as post-install and post-upgrade Helm hooks, and
nova-compute's init container lists both as kubernetes-entrypoint
dependencies. Helm runs the readiness wait before the post-upgrade hook
phase, so with disableWait: false the newly created nova-compute pods
block on jobs Helm has not created yet while Helm blocks on those pods,
and the release deadlocks until the timeout. This is scale-independent
and would deadlock on a single-node system. With no wait available to
restore, a percentage would only shorten the window in which the
application is misreported as applied, so it yields nothing here and is
left out until the hook coupling is addressed.

The remaining releases that carry disableWait: true are untouched.
Their reasons predate this defect and are not recorded, nova excepted,
so each of the others needs its own assessment.

No HelmRelease timeout or interval value changes. Readiness and
liveness probe settings are unchanged and min_ready_seconds stays at 0.
The Deployment rolling-update path is untouched; its replica counts
track controllers rather than compute nodes and it has no equivalent
exposure. Because a percentage rounds up with a floor of one, systems
with one or two compute nodes resolve to 1 and behave exactly as
before, so no special case is needed for AIO configurations. Absolute
concurrency does grow with node count, which is deliberate: 10% is two
nodes at twenty and twenty nodes at two hundred.

timeout, so the wait no longer causes the failure it was introduced to
avoid. Both the kstatus poller strategy and Helm's built-in readiness
check treat a DaemonSet as ready only when the observed generation
matches and updatedNumberScheduled and numberReady equal
desiredNumberScheduled [3], so the wait is correct under either
strategy and no custom health-check expressions are needed.

These two charts are the ones where parallelising is safe, because
their pods are node-local. Neither holds state that another chart's
pods depend on mid-rollout, so replacing eleven at once is eleven
independent restarts rather than a fleet-wide event. Instance
connectivity is not carried by either: measured across a full rollout,
libvirt produced zero failed TCP connections in 52481 samples and
pci-irq-affinity-agent zero in 83221.

Template updateStrategy and minReadySeconds in the
pci-irq-affinity-agent chart. It emitted no updateStrategy at all, so
the rendered object fell back to the Kubernetes default of
maxUnavailable: 1 and no override could reach it. The failure mode was
silent: an override was accepted and displayed by helm-override-show
while the rendered DaemonSet stayed unchanged. The chart default is
left at max_unavailable: 1, so the template change alone is
behaviour-neutral and only makes the value reachable; the value itself
comes from the static overrides.

Express max_unavailable as 10% on ceilometer without changing its
disableWait. This value has no effect on the currently supported
update source, where the compute DaemonSet does not exist and is
therefore created rather than rolled. It is set here because recovery
applies the charts of the release being recovered to, so the value
shipped in this release paces both the next forward rollout and a
rollback into this release: roughly three hours of the application
being reported applied while pods cycle at 1, against under twenty
minutes at 10%. It cannot breach a timeout, because this release keeps
disableWait: true and nothing waits on the rollout.

Declare libvirt as a dependency of the nova release. nova-compute's
init container already lists a same-host libvirt pod with
requireSameNode: true, so without this edge the two releases are
unordered siblings under placement, Flux reconciles them concurrently,
and a nova pod can land on a node whose libvirt pod is mid-replacement
and stall until it becomes ready. The edge makes the release graph
express a dependency the charts already have. It is safe in every
supported configuration because libvirt has no _is_enabled override
and never removes its own HelmRelease, so the target always exists
wherever nova is deployed, and it holds regardless of nova's own
disableWait because dependsOn gates on the dependency. Its cost is
that pci-irq-affinity-agent, which depends on nova, starts about
twelve minutes later.

The rule this establishes, and the one every release touched here now
satisfies: a DaemonSet release either waits and is parallelised, or
does not wait and stays serial. The combination shipped previously,
serial and not waiting, is the one that produces a multi-hour rollout
reported as complete on arrival.

Because a percentage rounds up with a floor of one, systems with one
or two compute nodes resolve to 1 and behave exactly as before, so no
special case is needed for AIO configurations. Absolute concurrency
does grow with node count, which is deliberate: 10% is two nodes at
twenty and twenty at two hundred.

openvswitch is deliberately left unscaled, and the reason is service
impact rather than timeout. Restarting an openvswitch pod interrupts
instance connectivity on that node for 2.2 to 3.8 seconds, because the
OVS kernel datapath keeps forwarding on cached flows while
ovs-vswitchd restarts. That cost is per-node and is already paid on
every update today. But when a node has its openvswitch and
neutron-ovs-agent pods replaced within about sixteen seconds of each
other, the datapath loses its userspace flow state while the agent
that would reprogram it is also unavailable, and connectivity is
interrupted for 25 to 30 seconds instead. Exposure is a function of
how much of the openvswitch rollout overlaps neutron's: at three hours
only a small part of the run overlaps neutron's fifteen minutes and
roughly one node is affected, but compressed to eighteen minutes
nearly every node's replacement falls inside neutron's window, and the
figure measured at 102-node scale was about 11%. Ordering the two
releases removes the interaction rather than reducing its probability,
so scaling this chart is deferred to the change that lands that
ordering.

A dependsOn from neutron to openvswitch is not that ordering, and this
change does not add one. When OVS runs with DPDK the dataplane is
managed on the host and the openvswitch chart is not deployed at all:
OpenvswitchHelm._is_enabled returns False and execute_kustomize_updates
then calls helm_release_resource_delete, removing the HelmRelease from
the kustomization. A dependsOn entry naming a HelmRelease that does
not exist leaves the dependent release permanently unreconciled, so
the application apply would never complete on a DPDK deployment. The
two conditions do not overlap, since the interaction requires a
containerised openvswitch pod, which is exactly the configuration in
which the dependency would be valid, so a conditional edge added under
the same predicate that governs the chart is correct rather than a
compromise. It needs a dependency-removal method alongside
helm_release_resource_delete in sysinv/helm/kustomize_base.py and an
execute_kustomize_updates hook in the neutron plugin, neither of which
exists yet. Both files carry comments recording this.

The neutron agents are left at max_unavailable: 1, and not because
they fit the timeout. Whether they fit is configuration-dependent: the
largest agent group on the measured system was 62 pods and finished in
about 16 minutes, but that system splits its compute nodes across
groups, and a homogeneous 100-node system puts all of them in one
group at roughly 35 minutes, which breaches the 30m timeout. The
durable reason is that unlike libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent the
neutron agents are not node-local in what they serve: l3-agent and
dhcp-agent own routers and networks, and with
max_l3_agents_per_router: 1 and l3_ha: false each router has exactly
one agent hosting it. Eleven concurrent replacements is therefore
eleven routers losing their only agent, not eleven independent
restarts. Scaling these needs per-agent treatment, which this change
does not attempt.

nova keeps disableWait: true and max_unavailable: 1. nova-db-sync and
nova-rabbit-init are declared as post-install and post-upgrade Helm
hooks, and nova-compute's init container lists both as
kubernetes-entrypoint dependencies. Helm runs the readiness wait
before the post-upgrade hook phase, so with disableWait: false the
newly created nova-compute pods block on jobs that Helm has not
created yet while Helm blocks on those pods, and the release deadlocks
until the timeout. This is scale-independent and would deadlock on a
single-node system, so nova can yield no status-accuracy improvement
until the hook coupling is addressed. Scaling it alone would only
shorten the window in which it is misreported, which is the property
this change is trying to remove rather than shorten, so it is left at
1 and the HelmRelease carries a comment recording the constraint. The
general form of the constraint: a DaemonSet may take
disableWait: false only if no init-container dependency resolves to a
resource created in that same release's post-upgrade hook phase.

The remaining releases carrying disableWait: true are untouched. Their
reasons predate this defect and are not recorded, nova and ceilometer
excepted, so each needs its own assessment.

Readiness and liveness probe settings are unchanged, min_ready_seconds
stays at 0, and no HelmRelease timeout or interval value changes. The
Deployment rolling-update path is untouched; its replica counts track
controllers rather than compute nodes and it has no equivalent
exposure.

Test Plan:

Percentage resolution and chart rendering, verified against the built
application tarball:
  PASS - pci-irq-affinity-agent renders maxUnavailable: 1 as an
         integer from the chart default
  PASS - the static override sets max_unavailable at the same values
         path the template reads, pod.lifecycle.upgrades.daemonsets
         .pci_irq_affinity_agent, and resolves to "10%"
  PASS - updateStrategy and minReadySeconds omitted when the entry is
         disabled
  PASS - rollingUpdate block omitted when pod_replacement_strategy is
         not RollingUpdate
  PASS - rendered output byte-identical to the pre-change chart when
         defaults are used
  PASS - a 102-pod DaemonSet resolves 10% to 11
  PASS - an 8-pod host group resolves 10% to 1, confirming round-up
         with a floor of one
  PASS - a 14-pod host group resolves 10% to 2
  PASS - percentage accepted as a string by the IntOrString field
  PASS - shipped manifests carry the intended values and nothing else:
         libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent at disableWait false with
         10%, ceilometer at disableWait true with 10%, openvswitch
         nova and neutron at disableWait true with 1
  PASS - the added dependsOn edge introduces no cycle; verified across
         all 29 releases, nova moves to depth 9 and
         pci-irq-affinity-agent to depth 10

Standard configuration, 2 controllers, 102 openstack-labelled compute
nodes, rollout duration and concurrency:
  PASS - libvirt full rollout in 11m45s at 11 concurrent, against a
         predicted 12.3m, from a 2h06m baseline
  PASS - pci-irq-affinity-agent full rollout in 18m32s at 11
         concurrent, against a predicted 21.2m
  PASS - both waiting charts complete inside the 30m HelmRelease
         timeout
  PASS - per-pod cycle time does not degrade with concurrency;
         measured wave intervals were below the single-replacement
         baseline on both charts
  PASS - instances remain ACTIVE throughout both rollouts

Instance impact on the same configuration, probed by TCP connect at
sub-second resolution:
  PASS - libvirt, zero failed connections across 52481 samples during
         a full rollout
  PASS - pci-irq-affinity-agent, zero failed connections across 83221
         samples during a full rollout
  PASS - neutron-ovs-agent replaced alone, no measurable interruption
  PASS - openvswitch replaced alone, 2.2 to 3.8 seconds per node,
         matching the single-replacement baseline and unchanged by
         this review since the chart is not scaled

Status accuracy on the same configuration:
  <TO BE COMPLETED FROM THE UPGRADE RUN - see the four items below.
   nova, ceilometer and openvswitch are excluded: they keep
   disableWait: true and therefore still report Ready before their
   rollouts have completed.>
  - libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent report READY=True only after
    their DaemonSets report updatedNumberScheduled equal to
    desiredNumberScheduled
  - sysinv reports the application applying until both rollouts have
    completed
  - the apply-in-progress alarm stays raised for the duration
  - host-unlock and host-swact continue to be rejected while those
    rollouts are in flight

Failure handling:
  <TO BE COMPLETED - a libvirt pod forced into a crash loop must cause
   the release to report a failure and the apply to fail, and the
   existing recovery path must restore the previous version>

Regression:
  PASS - neutron agents unchanged at max_unavailable: 1 and unaffected
  PASS - openvswitch unchanged; comment-only edit to its HelmRelease
  PASS - neutron unchanged; comment-only edit to its HelmRelease
  PASS - nova max_unavailable and disableWait unchanged; the only
         functional edit is the added dependsOn
  PASS - ceilometer disableWait unchanged at true
  PASS - the remaining releases carrying disableWait unchanged
  PASS - HelmRelease timeout and interval values unchanged
  PASS - Deployment rolling-update values unchanged
  PASS - unlabelled compute nodes excluded from all these DaemonSets
  PASS - instances on nodes outside the current wave keep
         uninterrupted connectivity
  SKIP* - AIO-SX and two-node configurations

* Not exercised on a single-node or two-node system. The
  floor-of-one behaviour those configurations rely on is covered by
  the 8-pod host group result above, which resolves 10% to 1.

References:
[1] DaemonSet maxUnavailable percentages round up against
    status.desiredNumberScheduled
    https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/daemon-set-v1/
[2] Deployment maxUnavailable rounds down while maxSurge rounds up,
    the opposite convention, which is why the two paths cannot share a
    value
    https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/
[3] helm-controller HelmRelease v2 spec, install and upgrade
    disableWait, dependsOn, and the wait strategy
    https://github.com/fluxcd/helm-controller/blob/main/docs/spec/v2/helmreleases.md
